Dear Northwestern Community,
We are pleased to present the fifth edition of the Northwestern Undergraduate Research
Journal (NURJ). As part of Northwesterns distinguished research community, NURJ aims to foster the
opportunity for outstanding undergraduate researchers to publish their work and share their findings
with the broader Northwestern community and to promote more cohesive communication across
academic disciplines.
In the past year, the NURJ executive board expanded our involvement in the undergraduate
research community. This year, not only did we recruit and receive strong submissions from a broader
range of academic fields previously unrepresented in our journal (including history and anthropol-
ogy), but also we expanded our programs to include a quarterly newsletter designed to give Northwest-
ern undergraduates a wider exposure to the exemplary research community on campus.
The fifth edition of the Northwestern Undergraduate Research Journal has been made possible
by the incredible dedication and hard work of many individuals. We would like to extend our gratitude
to all of the authors and contributing writers for taking the time and effort to submit such high-quality
work. In addition we would like to extend our deepest thanks to all of our faculty and student review-
ers, without whom our editorial review process would be inconceivable. Finally, we would like to thank
the staff and executive board of NURJ for their efforts and dedication to producing a high-quality
journal.
Sincerely,
Danwen Song

FEATURE
Economic Stimulus Means More Opportunity,
More Research for NU
JESSICA GOTTESMAN
D
espite the economic recession, the influx of Northwestern Universitys proposals for science
research is at an all time high. Due to the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA)
signed by President Obama on February 17th of this year,  opportunities for short-term
economy-stimulating research have received a record boost.
Allotting $10 billion to NIH for health research and refurbishing of their facili-
ties, $3 billion to NSF for basic science and engineering, $1 billion to NASA, as well as $1.6
billion to agencies ranging from climate science to nuclear physics, these grants are structured
differently from those previously offered. In order to aid in economic recovery, the funds are to be awarded almost
immediately instead of in gradual stages, many stipulate that the research must be completed within two years, and
all require the researches to report on their progress four times a year instead of annually. Considering the enormous
turnout from researchers, most people dont seem to mind navigating a few new requirements. In fact, the scale of
the competition poses the greatest challenge to Northwesterns benefiting from the stimulus plan.
Susan Ross, director of Sponsored Research at Northwestern, admits that the success rate for accepted
proposals is expected to be low. For the NIHs April Challenge Grant deadline, the agency intended to award 200
proposals, including a small percentage of prior submissions they had on file. More than 200 new proposals were
sent out from Northwestern alone, competing against institutions from around the country.
Despite the adversaries, Northwestern is determined to be among the most competitive, and working
equally hard on this front is Dr. Holly Falk-Krzesinski, Academic Director for the Office of Research Development.
My job is to make sure Northwestern gets more than its fair share, she notes. Weve really encouraged researchers
to send in proposals. Beyond the hope of success, however, Dr. Falk-Krzesinski also observes that putting together
the proposals are good experiences for the researchers, no matter the result. The efforts have increased cooperation
and collaboration among departments at Northwestern as Kellogg, SESP, the Law school, Medill, and others have
partnered with schools like Feinberg to create joint projects.
The stimulus for scientific research, while generally considered a positive strategy, has also created a number

of problems. As federal agencies scramble to review new projects, the details are often not as thoroughly worked out
as they have been for previous grants, leading to confusion on the part of institutions as well as contradictory feed-
back and guidance from the agencies. Nevertheless, contends Dr. Falk-Krzesinski, the atmosphere remains optimis-
tic. Folks at these federal agencies have been incredibly responsive and helpful in working with us, she says, though
having to clear up these problems on top of organizing the flurry of new proposals and questions has only added to
the number of overtime hours she and others in her office are putting in.
This is all happening incredibly quickly in terms of how government agencies and universities normally
work, Ross said over the phone as she dashed home to pack and catch a flight for another meeting. Its put a huge
stress on the system. Ross had people working 7 days a week to prepare for the Challenge Grant deadline in April,
and with a new NIH deadline approaching and weekly deadlines from various other organizations, theres no end
in sight. Thus far, the effort seems to be paying off. Every proposal turned into their office was successfully finalized
and submitted by the deadline. Meanwhile, in between teaching both in Evanston and downtown, Dr. Falk-Krzesin-
ski constantly updates her departments website and sends out notification emails through a special listserv. People
in her office joke, Were not sure if this has stimulated the economy, but its definitely stimulated more work.
Still, more work doesnt necessarily translate into generating new jobs at Northwestern. Though the staff
works overtime, Northwestern has no immediate plans to hire new employees. We have to balance that against the
fact that the endowments down and Northwesterns working hard not to lay people off, stresses Dr. Falk-Krzesinski,
but she notes that as proposals are accepted, new jobs may be in store for the future. Awarded investigators are ex-
pected to apply for supplemental grants to cover lab technicians, pay researchers, fund graduate research, and cover
equipment costs. This is good news for high school
students and undergraduates as well, who will not only
have more opportunities to fund their own research
projects, but will be able to find new lab opportunities
available to aid researchers.
Dr. Falk-Krzesinski adds with confidence,
Northwestern expects to do well. Were committed to
the end.
Many thanks to Susan Ross and Dr. Holly Falk-Krzesinski
for their information and support in creating this article,
especially at this busy time.

FEATURE
Breast Cancer and Early Development
NOEL SLESINGER
T
hey grow up so fast. It seems to be a common sentiment among the older
generation, especially as they watch the children in their lives grow up in an
age dominated by technology and easily accessible information on almost any
topic. However, recent studies have shown that girls are not just growing up
faster mentally, but physically as well.
Normally, puberty begins for girls around the age of ten. However,
many girls have been showing the first sign of puberty, breast development, at
the age of nine, especially girls with a Body Mass Index that falls in the obese range. Dr. Joyce Lee
of the University of Michigan reported to BBC News, Previous studies had found that girls who
have earlier puberty tend to have higher body mass index, but it was unclear whether puberty led
to the weight gain or weight gain led to the earlier onset of pubertyOur study offers evidence
that it is the latter. One explanation for this early onset places the hormone leptin, which is
produced by fat tissue and triggers puberty, as the culprit. Another fifteen year study by the
University of Copenhagen theorizes that exposure to endocrine-disrupting chemicals is to blame.
Both of these studies show, though, that no matter what the cause, the age for entering puberty is
changing.
But that leaves the question: Why is one year so important?  The problem is that early
puberty has been linked to a number of physical and social problems. Early development has
been linked with depression, and girls who enter puberty earlier are more prone to engage in
high-risk behavior. Also, girls who developed early have a higher risk of diabetes later in life.
One theory is that, because breast tissue has been shown to be sensitive to hormones, it makes
it highly resistant to insulin. Furthermore, because girls who are obese tend to have more breast
tissue, they are put at a higher risk for diabetes.
Not only do girls who develop early have a higher risk of diabetes, they also have a higher
risk of developing breast cancer. Like diabetes, though, hormones may play a part. Estrogen, the
hormone that plays a role in breast development and growth by stimulating breast cell division,
has been shown to be one of the factors involved in the development of breast cancer. Because it
supports the growth of estrogen-responsive tumors, women who have had a higher exposure to
estrogen may have a higher risk of developing breast cancer. As girls enter puberty earlier, they
are exposed to estrogen for longer periods of time, which may put them at risk for breast cancer
later in life.
What has many researchers worried is what this change might mean for the larger
population. As Dr. Lise Aksglaede of Copenhagen University Hospital told The New York Times,
Changes in development, such as early puberty, might reflect changes in the general health in
a population. However, nothing has been proven yet, and, when it comes to breast cancer and
other health risks, other factors-- such as environment, health, and geneticscannot be ignored.
Research continues to investigate the causes as to why breast development has changed so rapidly
as well as the consequences it may entail. While researchers continue to look for answers to these
complicated questions, to quote Dr. Askglaede, Probably the majority of these girls will mature
without any side effects. The problem is that we do not know.

The Skinny on Stress:
Maternal Psychosocial Stress and Birth
Weight in the Philippines
LDEPARTMENT
AURA M. ROGERS
OF ANTHROPOLOGY
THOMAS MCDADE
FACULTY ADVISOR, DEPARTMENT OF
ANTHROPOLOGY, NORTHWESTERN
UNIVERSITY
L
Low birth weight is a major cause of perinatal mortality and childhood morbidity and it has also been found to increase disease risk in adulthood and decrease
fecundity. Despite previous birth weight research and nutritional intervention
programs, the proportion of the world’s low birth weight infants has changed
little in the past 30 years (Phung et al., 2003). The purpose of this study is to
explore the influence of maternal psychosocial stress on birth weight in a large
population-based cohort of Filipino women and their infants (n=2891). Measures of maternal psychosocial stress from economic stressors, life event stressors,
home stressors and work stressors were collected during pregnancy. These stress
measurements were combined to create a continuous measurement of maternal
psychosocial stress, ranging from 0 stressors to 8 stressors, which was used to
predict infant birth weight. After accounting for alternate variables that influence
birth weight, each psychosocial stressor that mothers suffered during pregnancy
was found to decrease their infants’ birth weights by 27 grams and increase the
likelihood of low birth weight classification by 15%. These findings suggest an
effect of maternal psychological health on birth weight.
INTRODUCTION
ow birth weight is a health concern on
a global scale.  According to the World
Health Organization, the birth weight
of an infant is the single most impor-
tant determinant of its chances of sur-
vival and healthy growth and develop-
ment (WHO, 1984).  Low birth weight is a major cause
of perinatal mortality and morbidity and it has been
linked to a multitude of health problems throughout
the entire life cycle (Bryant Borders et al, 2007). During
childhood, low birth weight infants have an increased
risk for illnesses, subnormal growth, and neurodevelop-
mental issues including problems in cognition, atten-
tion, and neuromotor functioning (Hack et al., 1995).
Despite attempts to decrease the prevalence of low birth
weight through research of the risk factors and nutri-
tional interventions, the proportion of the worlds low
birth weight infants has changed little in the past 30
years (Phung et al., 2003).
Low birth weight has been defined as a birth
weight of less than 2500 grams, up to and including
2499 grams (WHO, 1984).  Due to the popularity of low
birth weight research, a number of maternal variables
have been found to significantly influence birth weight.
Maternal nutritional status is strongly predictive of
infant birth weight (Thame et al, 1997).  Additionally, a
number of nonnutritional maternal variables have been
found to influence birth weight.  They include primi-
parity (Phung et al, 2003), prenatal care (Guilkey et al.,
1989), illness and infection (Heinke and Kuzawa, 2008),
age and addictive behaviors (Phung, 2003), ethnicity
(Roberts, 1997), socioeconomic status (Hughes, 1995),
and psychosocial stress (Bryant Borders, 2007).
Psychosocial stress has been analyzed as a
potential cause of low birth weight for almost 50 years
(Davids et al, 1961). In a study of 117 women at an
urban medical center in the United States, a relationship
was found between life stress, calculated by adding the
events that the mother rated as bad events in her life,
and low birth weight (Norbeck and Tilden, 1983). In
a prospective study of 294 pregnant women receiving
welfare in Illinois, chronic stressors such as food inse-
curity, unemployment, and crowding in the home, were
also found to predict low birth weight (Bryant Borders,

The purpose of this study is to explore the in-

The analyses aim to determine whether mothers who
experience more psychosocial stressors will give birth to
infants with lower birth weight than mothers who are
not psychosocially stressed.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Study population
This study uses data from an ongoing, community-
based, prospective study, the Cebu Longitudinal Health
and Nutrition Survey (CLHNS). The study site is
Metropolitan Cebu, an area that encompasses the City
of Cebu and rural districts on the central Philippines
island of Cebu (Guilkey et al., 1989). The CLHNS is a 1-
year birth cohort that originally enrolled 3,327 pregnant
women from May 1, 1983 to April 30, 1984. In most
cases, baseline interviews with the mothers took place
between 26 and 34 weeks gestation.

Statistical analysis
Maternal psychosocial stress was coded on a scale from
0 to 8 based on the number of stressors reported (0=no
stressors, 1=1 stressor8=8 stressors). Birth weight
was analyzed as a continuous variable. A series of linear
and logistic models were run, beginning with simple

weight. Variables were added progressively to the regres-
sion that could confound the association, or that might
be a causal pathway, including gestational age at birth,
mothers nutritional status, measured by height, caloric
intake, and maternal triceps skinfold thickness, primi-
parity, number of prenatal visits, mothers age, illness
during pregnancy, and smoking during pregnancy. All
analyses were performed with version 10 of Stata (Stata
Corporation, College Station, TX). Analyses and models
were restricted to the subsample of mothers and infants

RESULTS
Data collection
All data were obtained under conditions of informed
consent with human subject clearance from the Univer-
sity of North Carolina, Chapel Hill and the University
of San Carlos (Adair and Popkin, 1988). Information
on maternal health, lifestyle and environment were ob-
tained during the baseline interview in the respondents
homes. Maternal anthropometrics (height, weight,
and triceps skinfold thickness) were measured using
standard techniques. Birth weight data for infants born
in hospitals was measured by birth attendants using
hospital scales, while birth weight data for infants born
at home was measured by birth attendants who were
trained in the use of Salter hanging-type scales (Heinke
and Kuzawa, 2008).
The prevalence of maternal psychosocial
stressors was assessed during the baseline interview in
the second or third trimester of pregnancy. Women
were defined as economically stressed if their income
or household assets were in the lowest quartile of the
sample. They were defined as stressed at home if their
time spent on housework and household crowding
values were in the highest quartile. Women were defined
as stressed at work if their place of work was outside
the barangay, a Filipino term for village, or they were
unable to care for their children while at work. Finally,
they were defined as stressed by negative life events if

Examining the effects of predator exclusion
structures associated with geoduck aquaculture on mobile
benthic macrofauna in South Puget Sound, Washington
RDEPARTMENT
ACHEL SMITH
OF BIOLOGY
P. SEAN MCDONALD
FACULTY ADVISOR, SCHOOL OF AQUATIC
AND FISHERY SCIENCES, UNIVERSITY OF
WASHINGTON
NATIONAL SCIENCE FOUNDATION RESEARCH
EXPERIENCES FOR UNDERGRADUATES
PROGRAM, SHANNON POINT MARINE
CENTER, ANACORTES, WASHINGTON
T

Intertidal aquaculture of geoduck clams (Panopea abrupta) is a rapidly expanding industry in Puget Sound, Washington, yet little is known about the ecological impacts of disturbances associated with geoduck operations. This study
examined the effects of predator exclusion structures associated with geoduck
aquaculture on mobile benthic macrofauna in South Puget Sound, Washington. Species abundance and diversity were assessed on both structured and
unstructured habitats; surveys revealed significantly more graceful crab (Cancer
gracilis) on unstructured habitats, and significantly more Pacific staghorn sculpin
(Leptocottus armatus) on structured habitats. Dietary patterns of L. armatus
occupying both habitats were evaluated in relation to tide level. Stomachs of
L. armatus were significantly more full on ebbing than flooding tides for both
habitats, suggesting that sculpin migrate into intertidal areas to forage. However,
results for small sculpin (52-81 mm TL) were equivocal, and these fish may use the
complex structured habitat for refuge in addition to foraging. A significant difference in prey composition was observed between habitats, which is attributed to
increased variability of prey on the structured habitat. Infaunal polychaetes were
the main prey in unstructured habitats, while sculpin consumed more epibenthic
gammarids in structured habitats. Predator exclusion structures used in geoduck
aquaculture appear to alter the composition of macrofaunal communities relative to unstructured areas and affect the dietary patterns of L. armatus.
INTRODUCTION
he Pacific geoduck, Panopea abrupta,
is a large clam found in the intertidal
and subtidal substrates of the north-
eastern Pacific1. The geoducks soft,
fleshy body and siphon have great
commercial value, with Asian markets
fetching prices of up to $30 per pound2. With a market
already estimated at $80 million in Washington and
British Columbia2, geoduck aquaculture has become an
increasingly lucrative industry in South Puget Sound,
Washington. Although a great deal of work has been
done to explore the environmental impacts of other
types of bivalve aquaculture3,4,5, little research has yet
been done to determine the effects of geoduck aquacul-
ture on benthic communities as commercial geoduck
operations are a relatively new industry1.
Geoduck aquaculture involves several proce-
dures that may impact benthic communities. This proj-
ect focuses on the disturbance associated with the place-
ment of predator exclusion structures on the tidelands
at the beginning of the geoduck harvest cycle. Juvenile
geoducks are out-planted into polyvinylchloride (PVC)
tubes that are stomped into the intertidal zone. The
tubes are covered with netting and the structures are left
on the tidelands for approximately two years, or until
the geoducks have reached significant size refuge from
predation. The placement of these artificial structures in
the intertidal zone increases the structural complexity of
the habitat; the novel substrate created by the predator
exclusion structures may provide additional attach-
ment surfaces for epibiota and thus alter the community
assemblage relative to natural soft-bottom substrate6,7.
Moreover, the increased complexity of the habitat pro-
vided by the predator exclusion structures may attract
organisms that would not otherwise colonize the area8,
altering microhabitat composition and changing forag-
ing and migratory behavior of intertidal macrofauna
predators9.
This work examines the abundance and diet
of two mobile migratory species, graceful crab Cancer
gracilis and Pacific staghorn sculpin Leptocottus arma-
tus, on structured and unstructured habitats. Both C.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
Study Site
The study was conducted in South Puget Sound, Wash-
ington during the summer of 2008. Three active geo-
duck aquaculture sites were chosen for observation: the
Butson, Totten, and Scarf sites (Fig.1). Each owned and
operated by Taylor Shellfish Company, all study sites
included aquaculture sections planted with geoducks
protected by predator exclusion structures in addition
to adjacent sections of unstructured habitat planted
with mature geoducks.
Trapping Survey
RESEARCH
A trapping survey was performed at all three sites to
assess the composition of mobile macrofauna utilizing
littoral habitats at high tide. Baited traps were placed
on both structured and unstructured habitats during
low tide, and left overnight for 24 hours. 15 traps were
placed in arrays on both habitats of the Butson site, and
10 traps were placed on both habitats of the Lev and
Scarf sites. The traps were retrieved the following day at
low tide, and the number, size, and species of captured
macrofauna were recorded. The mean catch of the two
most prevalent species, C. gracilis, and L. armatus, was
analyzed in two separate 2-way ANOVA tests, with site
and habitat as factors.
Stomach Content Analysis
To determine the effects of predator exclusion struc-
tures on the diets of benthic macrofauna, L. armatus
and C. gracilis were captured with a pole seine net on
the structured and unstructured habitats at the Butson
site on both ebb and flood tides. Captured fish and
crabs were measured, and in the lab, diet patterns of L.
armatus were examined using methods modified from
Armstrong et al. (1995)13. Stomachs were extracted from
preserved L. armatus samples (n = 113), relative stom-
ach fullness was determined, and stomach contents were
examined and separated into distinct prey groups that
were then individually weighed to determine individual
diet contributions. Food items were identified to the
lowest taxonomic level, and grouped into prey catego-
ries by frequency of occurrence. The stomach con-
tent data was analyzed as in Armstrong et al. (1995)13
through a calculation of the Index of Relative Impor-
tance (IRI) for the individual prey categories.
Samples were also grouped by fish length and
separated into two size classes: small (52-81 mm) and
large (82-147 mm). The mg of prey consumed per gram
of fish was calculated for structured and unstructured
habitats on both flood and ebb tides for large and
small sculpin, and data was analyzed with a multi-way
ANOVA with habitat, tide, and size as factors. The
prey data was also compared via multivariate analyses
using the PRIMER TM software package. Statistical dif-
ferences in prey composition between structured and
unstructured habitats were determined with analysis of
similarity (ANOSIM), and similarity percentages (SIM-
PER) analysis was used to quantify the contribution
of individual prey categories to differences highlighted
with ANOSIM.
RESULTS
Trapping Data
C. gracilis and L. armatus were the primary species cap-
tured. The mean number of C. gracilis caught per trap
at all three sites varied significantly between structured
and unstructured habitats (F=123.126, P <0.001), with
a significantly greater mean catch on the unstruc-
tured habitat than on the structured habitat (Fig. 2).
The mean number of L. armatus per trap also varied
significantly between structured and unstructured
habitats (F=20.253, P < 0.001), and the mean catch of
L. armatus was significantly higher on structured than
unstructured habitats (Fig. 2).

DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS
Evidence from the present study suggests that the preda-
tor exclusion structures placed in the intertidal zone
at the beginning of the geoduck aquaculture cycle may
affect macrofaunal communities, altering migratory
and dietary patterns of mobile fish and invertebrates.
Significantly more C. gracilis were observed on unstruc-
tured habitats than structured habitats and significantly
more L. armatus were observed on structured habitats
than unstructured habitats. Intertidal migration may
serve various purposes for macrofauna; individuals may
migrate to increase foraging opportunities, to decrease
agonistic activity, or to increase reproductive output9,15.
C. gracilis, may preferentially migrate into unstruc-
tured intertidal areas to forage9,16, as the limited habitat
complexity of the unstructured habitat may increase
foraging efficiency and predation17. Although struc-
turally complex areas may have higher prey densities
than less complex areas15, C. gracilis may be deterred
from migrating into these areas by reduced foraging
efficiency or by stranding risk of the predator exclusion
structures at low tide. The observation of significantly
more L. armatus on structured habitats than in un-
structured habitats is consistent with past studies of L.
armatus that observed a preference of sculpin for more

complex habitats14. There was a statistically significant
difference in the standardized weight (mg prey g-1 fish)
of L. armatus observed between ebb and flood tides for
both structured and unstructured habitats, with greater
stomach fullness on the ebb than the flood tide. Because
sculpin are entering littoral areas with empty stomachs
and leaving with full stomachs, it is suggested that
sculpin are migrating into the intertidal zone to forage.
This relationship between tide level and standardized
weight was strongest in the unstructured habitats, and
there was less difference in fullness between the tides in
the structured habitat, suggesting that migration into
the structured habitat may serve another purpose in
addition to foraging.
Division of the pooled data based upon fish
size suggests that L. armatus may be migrating into
structured areas in order to seek refuge. When examin-
ing the standardized weights for large fish, as for the
pooled data, fuller stomachs were observed on ebb tides
and emptier stomachs on flood tides. Interestingly, this
relationship does not hold for small fish. Small fish were
observed to have fuller stomachs on the flood tide and
emptier stomachs on the ebb tide. The higher predation
risk faced by small fish in conjunction with this obser-
vation suggests that L. armatus may find some refuge
value in the predator exclusion structures and may
migrate into these areas to reduce predation risk.
Prey composition of L. armatus was signifi-
cantly different between habitats, as the result of greater
overall variability in the diet of L. armatus on the struc-
tured habitat. The greater diversity of prey available on
the more complex surface of the structured habitat is
consistent with previous studies correlating increased
complexity with increased diversity and density of
species18,19,20. The difference in prey composition was de-
pendent upon polychaetes being a significantly greater
food source for sculpin on unstructured habitats and
gammarid amphipods being a significantly greater food
source for sculpin on structured habitats. This differ-
ence is important, as the main contributors to the diet
of L. armatus on the unstructured habitat, polychaetes,
are infaunal, benthic species, while the largest con-
tributors on the structured habitat, mobile gammarid
amphipods, consist of a guild of epibenthic species that
would not be present in the area if it were not for the
complex habitat provided by the predator exclusion
structures.
The differences in habitat utilization and diet
composition of L. armatus between structured and
unstructured habitats suggest that the predator exclu-
sion structures of geoduck aquaculture do affect mobile
benthic macrofauna. As the geoduck industry expands,
it will be important to consider the implications of
altering the diet and migratory patterns of L. armatus
NORTHWESTERN UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH JOURNAL
and other ecologically and economically important
macrofauna. Future studies could develop bioenergetics
models of L. armatus to determine if there are benefits
to feeding on prey from structured versus unstructured
habitats. It would be interesting to see if there is an
advantage to utilization of one habitat over the other,
and to observe how differences between the two habitats
affect L. armatus populations and on a broader scale,
the community to which they belong.

My project extends the arguments of Susan Layton’s 1995 book Russian Literature and Empire: Conquest of the Caucasus from Pushkin to Tolstoy. While Layton
explores how literature of the Caucasian conquest helped shaped conceptions of
Russian nationality and statehood, this paper probes the corollary influences of
the war on literature and its associated criticism.
Textual presentations of the Caucasian theater contributed to the rise
of a literary perspective that emphasized individual consciousness and experiential authenticity within the dynamic progression of the conquest from 1817 to
1864. By contesting fanciful Caucasian storytelling traditions, these innovative
narrative methods opposed established conventions of romanticism affirming
instead emerging tenets of realism.
How then did Russian authors experience the Caucasus and how did
they convey their impressions to Russia’s educated elite? What sentiments did
writers express and how did their convictions serve to inspire more objective portrayals of the character’s unique deliberations within his complex environments?
This paper accordingly examines primary source literary accounts of
the conquest to investigate how narrative developments evolved within their
simultaneously changing historical contexts. While these works illustrate the
remarkable artistic imaginations of Alexander Pushkin, Alexander BestuzhevMarlinsky, and Mikhail Lermontov, they additionally demonstrate cumulatively
momentous transitions of descriptive procedure and form. While these three
authors subscribed to numerous and even opposing writing traditions, the sum
succession and consequences of their Caucasian works promoted a critical
legacy that endorsed realism as a preeminent literary style of modernity.
he Caucasus has been called a
dazzling mosaic of ethnic groups
and rival clans, a place where the
individual struggles with his concep-
tion of self  in response to conten-
tious considerations of Muslim vs.
Christian, Eastern vs. Western, and
Asian vs. European identities1. Divided by these fault
lines of civilizations, the Caucasian mountain range is
a borderland torn between the cultural and political
influences of different worlds . More than fifty different
indigenous peoples reside in the territory between the
Black and Caspian Seas, including Georgians, Circas-
sians, Chechens, Armenians, Dagestani, Iranians, and
Turks3. Russian military forces invaded and conquered
NORTHWESTERN UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH JOURNAL
the region between 1817 and 18644.
Texts describing the Caucasian conquest com-
municate the efforts and outlooks of one civilization
triumphing over another. Under the pretexts of nation,
empire, and ideology, the individual and his society
attempt to advance their own hegemonic ascendancies
over foreign, feebler others5. Expressing such attitudes
after his victorious military campaigns in Gaul, Gaius
Julius Caesar proclaimed veni, vidi, vici, to signify that
the Roman Empire as embodied in his own personage
came, saw and conquered the provinces inferior, un-
sophisticated barbarians6. Victors write the history that
reveres their own authority as superior to the claims of
subjugated counterparts7. But how are these minority
voices acknowledged and represented in the literature
of the vanquisher? And, how does the course of political
RESEARCH
and military affairs influence this dialogue?
While overarching national, imperial, and
ideological stimuli promoted the conquest, individu-
als also had specific, personal reasons to travel to the
Caucasian frontier. Sizeable Russian populations, for
example, came as civil servants, travelers, soldiers, and
exiles8. Political and criminal deportees arrived in such
great numbers that people started calling the territory
"southern Siberia" already in the time of Alexander I9.
Some of these individuals undertook literary endeavors
to describe their Caucasian experiences to influential
literate circles10. Though only an estimated 4 percent of
the male population in a certain province could read in
1844, this same minority represented Russias powerful,
educated, and governing elite11.
Authors participating in the state's expansion-
ary efforts surveyed the empires unknown corners, ob-
served foreign populations, and assigned them cultural
ranks in relation to their own societies12. Introducing
readers to territories whose geographical and ethnic
features were not yet sufficiently known to the nations
readership, Russian writers adapted a textual inter-
face with Europes renaissance orientale, concentrating
initially on the Crimean peninsula, a region seized from
Muslim Tatars in 178313. When Catherine the Great
traveled to the Crimea on an official state tour in 1787,
for instance, she announced the territory a fairy tale
land from The Thousand and One Nights14. Although at
first the Crimea intrigued readers with its aura of east-
ern exoticism, the Caucasus soon became the primary
setting of the Russian oriental domain15.
While numerous individuals reported the
events of the Caucasian conquest from 1817 to 1864,
this paper specifically analyzes the accounts of three
prominent Russian authors: Alexander Sergeyevich
Pushkin (1799-1837), Alexander Bestuzhev-Marlinsky
(1797-1837), and Mikhail Iur'vich Lermontov (1814-
1841)l6. Although they subscribed to numerous and
even opposing writing traditions, by emphasizing the
unique deliberations of the individual within his com-
plex environments, these three authors countered es-
tablished conventions of romanticism affirming instead
emerging narrative principles of realism.
No explicit break separated these two move-
ments, which makes the change harder to discern.
As the literary principles of realism and romanticism
evolved concurrently in the realm of Russian prose, they
competed for prominence, especially in texts describ-
ing the conquest of the Caucasus. As both military and
literary contests unfolded, the transition away from
romanticism towards realism occurred with a progres-
sion of hybrid texts employing methods and techniques
belonging to both narrative styles17. Blending the poetic
and the pragmatic, Russian writers attempted to make
their fictitious Caucasian tales more believable by pre-
senting facts and embellishments in tandem18.
Pushkins Caucasian texts, for instance,
received praise from his contemporary and succeed-
ing audiences for presenting purportedly authentic
geographical and ethnographic detail [with] technical
excellence of verse. instead of writing too didactically
and, perforce, too prosaically19. Authors describing the
conquest performed the interdisciplinary activities of
littérateur, journalist, and scientist in conveying their
observations and interpretations of the war to Russian
readers20. Although the three writers discussed in this
paper accommodated romantic elements in varying
degrees, their realist emphasis on the individuals con-
sciousness within his dynamic surroundings attained
more pronounced critical praise than their parallel
romantic methodologies.
Even though romanticism and realism seem
distinguishable, scholars continue to disagree over how
to properly classify certain authors and their works in
a particular narrative style. Elizabeth Cheresh Allen
explains in her 1992 book, Beyond Realism: Turgenevs
Poetics of Secular Salvation, that
[t]he trouble is most people, or at least most
students of realism, do not agree on the works
and authors that fall under its rubric. Snow, for
example, welcomes Dostoevsky and Tolstoy into
the Realist fold, whereas Erich Auerbach, author of
the magisterial study Mimesis: The Representation
of Reality in Western Literature, categorically refuses
to do so21.
This scholarly discord emerges from the historical
development of realism: the realist narrative style devel-
oped gradually over time with the efforts of numerous
writers participating in cross-cultural exchanges high-
lighting the keen observation of the individual within
his variegated circumstances.
Accordingly, definitions of realism tend to
rely on features that distinguish it from previous styles.
French modernist painter, Fernand Léger, for example,
argues "every epoch has its own realism, invented more
or less in relation to the preceding epochs22. George
Levine asserts supportively that what realism may be
at any moment depends both on what it has been and
what the culture expects it to be23. The blurring between
realism and romanticism has caused academics such
as Donald Fanger to uphold a "felicitous compromise
between moment and mode," evident in the title of his
1965 book, Dostoevsky and Romantic Realism24. The de-
scriptive conveyances of these two narrative forms can
at times seemingly coincide.
Despite the overlap of these literary

RESEARCH
movements, public acceptance of more objective narra-
tive procedures presented in accounts of the Caucasian
conquest advanced innovative approaches of realism at
the expense of foregoing conventions of romanticism.
Realist descriptions presented the setting of war more
legitimately and thereby usually more horrifically, while
romantic works falsely upheld its patriotic glorification.
As Russian military campaigns expanded into the Cau-
casus, Persia, and the Crimea, soldiers started perish-
ing in greater numbers. Mourning the deaths of family
members, loved ones, and fellow countrymen, readers
became dissatisfied romantic pomposity. The realist
narrative form, alternatively, empathized more sincerely
with peoples losses and effectively criticized the state's
overbearing imperial endeavors.
Correspondingly, although the three central
authors discussed in this paper contributed to the devel-
opment of realist approaches, their stories and literary
perspectives also accommodated romantic elements
some of these writers more so than others. While these
authors refuse definitively realist or romantic taxonomi-
cal categorizations, they undoubtedly cultivated a more
objective description of the character's unique perspec-
tive within his intricate surroundings.  In such regards,
the Caucasian works produced by these three prominent
authors promoted realist narrative approaches in the
face of adversity from embedded romantic literary con-
ventions.
Before understanding the traditions of realism
that emerged in accounts of the Caucasian conquest, it
is necessary to explore narrative styles that preceded it.
In his 1978 comparative study of Byron and Pushkin,
Victor Zhirmunsky categorized the romantic poema by
thematic and compositional features such as a disil-
lusioned hero, an exotic setting and fragmentariness25.
Moreover, romantic Caucasian stories entailed the
fanciful and fictitious, the visionary and impractical to
impart a tale of extravagant love, adventure, and excite-
ment26. As Russian readers gravitated more towards
emotional values rather than logical ones, skillful fic-
tional romantic presentations of the conquest received
immense popularity and public acclaim27.
Romantic narrative styles misrepresented the
Caucasian region with either tacit or explicit promo-
tions of the states imperial endeavors. As Vissarion
Belinsky affirmed in 1845, Caucasian literature appealed
unequivocally to Russian armchair travelers, who
exhibited an elevated readiness to enjoy the experience
of empire28. The elites sense of boredom made tales of
Caucasian freedom, adventure, and exoticism par-
ticularly appealing29. In this regard, romantic authors
draped the Caucasus in magic and mystery, utilizing hy-
perbole, and incredible outbursts of feeling to impress
audiences with the sensation of "reading as traveling30.

Along similarly persuasive lines, Russians pursued trav-
el as the antidote for the boredom ofmonotonous
life31." Calculated or not, the grandiose language of the
romantic approach inspired large numbers of Russians
to seek passage to the Caucasian frontier32.
Romantic accounts describing the conquest
breathed life into Caucasian rivers, cliffs, clouds, and
mountains, generating dialogues that read as brooding
parables on the themes of violent death, erotic longing,
and imperial encroachment33. The early 1814 episto-
lary verse, To Voeikov, by Vasili Andreevich Zhukovsky,
for instance, illustrated such romantic tendencies in its
presentation of the Caucasian mountaintop, Elbrus:
[a]nd like a cloud above the rest,/Elborus [sic] gleams
in all his glory/ [w]ith dreadful majesty-a hoary/[g]iant
capped by a double crest34. Zhukovsky had never even
travelled to the Caucasus when he wrote these verses
and based his portrayal on pure imagination35. Consid-
ering the ramifications of such ostentatious storytelling
practices, romantic writers bewildered expectations and
perceptions of the Caucasian setting.
Fear of penalty from the state contributed
to the general reticence about the nations imperial
endeavors. Under Tsar Nicholas I's regime (1825-1855),
the secret police became heavily involved in censor-
ship activities36. Opposing mandates and ideologies of
the autocratic regime could bring writers sentences of
house arrest, mandatory military service, forced labor,
imprisonment, exile, or death37.  Trepidation over au-
thoritarian censorship and punishment unquestionably
manipulated the formulation and distribution of
printed material.
Censor Alexander Nikitenko disparaged the
aims and implications of his own profession in his se-
cret 1826 diary. Referring to his nation's literate elite as
"rank automatons," Nikitenko described how "the guid-
ing principle...of the so-called high society....is not to
appear ridiculous. And not to appear ridiculous means
to conform slavishly to fashion in one's speech, opin-
ions and conduct38. As Nikitenkos sentiments confirm,
concessions made to the status quo, the comme il faut,
and the officially directed hegemonic claims of the Rus-
sian empire served to suppress the objective perspective
of the autonomous individual. Despite the excessive
efforts of the state to control the printed word, the voice
of the objective author endured39.
In several considerations, the methods of
realism addressed the overarching artistic and moral
shortcomings of romantic approaches widely purveyed
in Russian writing during the time period of the war.
Attempting to resolve romantic distortions and exag-
gerations, realism asserted unbiased transcriptions of
thought, observation, and experience40. Likewise, the
emerging tenets of realism affirmed an incurable love
RESEARCH
of the concrete and the verifiable, an instinctive distrust
of the abstract, the impalpable, and the supernatural,
while maintaining a scientific and positivist approach,
unfriendly to romanticism, intangible formulations,
and metaphysics41. Moreover, realist approaches main-
tained the individual was not merely a type, but rather
a specific, cognizant personality immersed within his
miscellaneous surroundings, upholding the study of
individuals everywhere as a worthwhile and informative
endeavor42. The astute description of every characters
distinct perspective encouraged increased self-aware-
ness, reflection, and deliberately considered action43.
The realist endorsement of individual objectivity over
subjectivity challenged established Russian literary and
political traditions throughout the progression of the
Caucasian conquest.
Throughout the conquest, Pushkin, Bestuzhev-
Marklinsky, and Lermontov all undertook initiatives to
underscore the significance of every character within his
complicated contexts. The works of these three authors
exhibited the rise of a realist narrative style that main-
tained the individual's autonomous weighing uncon-
strained by nationalistic, authoritarian influences. These
three authors challenged Russian readers to examine
more thoughtfully the conquest's actual occurrences
and implications.
The Caucasian texts of Alexander Sergeyevich
Pushkin (1799-1837), for instance, indicate the tran-
sition away from romanticism towards realism over
the course of the conquest's progression. Ultimately,
Pushkin's opinions and descriptions of the Caucasian
conquest appealed to an elite readership who opposed
estimations of western Europe as the apogee of world
civilization and voiced sensitivity to occidentalizations
negative impact44. To address this demographic of his
audience, Pushkin correspondingly voiced his praise
and admiration for the regions cultural traditions and
lifestyles to counter biased contemplations of Russian
superiority. In his glorification of Caucasian peoples,
Pushkin wrote in his 1822 Kavkazskiy plennik, (Pris-
oner of the Caucausus), The Circassian is covered with
arms;/ he is proud of them:/ on him there is armor, gun,
quiver,/Kuban saddle, dagger, lasso/ and shaska (sword),
his eternal companion/ for all labors and leisure45.
While he indeed made use of romantic literary tech-
niques, Pushkin expressed his wonder and veneration
for the regions proud and free peoples effectively break-
ing down the division between the Russian self and the
Caucasian other46.
Along similar lines, Pushkin mourned the sup-
pression of the territorys proud peoples, questioning
his own regard for the conquest in the passage,
did he regret days gone by,/ days of disap-
pointed hopes,/ or, curious, did he contem-
plate/amusements of bleak simplicity?/Did
he read in this faithful mirror/the habits of a
wild people?--/He hid the movements in his
heart/in deepest silence,/and on his high brow
nothing was betrayed47.
Reiterating comparable impressions of his Caucasian
experiences in an 1825 letter to his friend Nikolai
Raevsky, Pushkin asserted here you will find memo-
ries/ of days that were, perhaps, dear to the heart,/ the
contradictions of passions,/familiar dreams, familiar
sufferings/ and the secret voice of my soul48. While this
passage did not appear in publication, it still reflected
Pushkins meditations about the human and social
losses incurred in the civilizing process associated with
the conquest49. Pushkins eulogizing of Caucasian geog-
raphies and peoples lamented the Russian states efforts
to overpower them.
Still, Pushkins loyalty to Russian elites
made him an advocate of the colonial expansion in
the Caucasus and elsewhere50.  This solidarity caused
Pushkin to try to justify Russian atrocities through
referencing the tribesmens savagery51. Pushkin
expressed his outright support for the Russian
conquest of the Caucasus as a bloody but ultimately
benign necessity, writing in the epilogue of Prisoner of
the Caucasus, that
[t]he Caucasian region, the torrid boundary
of Asia, arouses interest in all respect.
Ermolov has filled it with his name and
beneficent genius. The savage Circassians have
become timorous; their ancient audacity is
disappearing. The roads are becoming less
dangerous by the hour, and the numerous
conveys are becoming superfluous.52.
Pushkins contrasting attitudes towards empire caused
his prose to fluctuate between elegiac mourning and
odic triumphalism53. His own internal divisions over
the necessity of the Caucasian conquest encouraged
the autonomous individual to participate in this line of
internal deliberating. Pushkin persuaded his readers to
decide for themselves how they felt about such issues54.
Alexander Bestuzhev-Marlinsky (1797-
1837) also emphasized Russians relationships to their
Caucasian counterparts in his 1830 story, Letters
from Dagestan. In this novella, Bestuzhev-Marlinsky
inferred repeatedly through rumors circulated amongst
troops that the adversarial Caucasian Prince, Gazi-
Muhammed, took on the external guise of Caucasian
identity only to veil his true personage as the grandson

RESEARCH
of a Russian turncoat embodying the offspring
of anti-Tsarist sentiment in [his] readerships own
country55. In such regards, Bestuzhev-Marlinsky
provoked his Russian literate audiences to reconsider
their own associations to Caucasian peoples effectively
countering prevailing discourses that degraded the
mountaineers as inferior savages56.
Bestuzhev first adapted the pseudonym
Marlinsky in an anonymous review of the tsars
government in 182057. His real identity only became
known to Russian audiences in 1837 when it was
announced that the generally forgotten Bestuzhev had
written many popular Caucasian tales of the 1830s
under the pseudonym Marlinsky58. The name Marlinsky
refers to the cultural fashions of marlinism, a highly
theatrical, melodramatic, and pseudoheroic mode of
behavior that arose in response to the pressures of post-
Decembrist Russia59. The connotations of his pen name
allude to his primarily romantic literary inclinations.
Of the three authors discussed in this paper,
Bestuzhev-Marlinsky represents the most categorically
romantic. Some might argue, for instance, that Pushkin
described the Caucasian setting more realistically than
did Bestuzhev-Marlinsky. Accordingly, Bestuzhev-
Marlinskys romantic proclivities reiterate that the
development of the realist narrative did not occur in
a gradual, linear chronological progression. Instead,
writers contributed to the rise of realism in hybrid texts
employing forms and methods from both movements,
albeit in varying degrees of authorial subscription to
one style or the other60.
In his 1834 text, however, Story of an Officer
Held Prisoner by Mountain Tribsemen, Bestuzhev-
Marlinsky provided realistic information about
the Caucasian region and its peoples. Warning
readers, not to dismiss these Caucasian peoples as
savages Bestuzhev-Marlinsky offered a trustworthy
ethnographic essay about a Dagestani tribe whose
community organization operated in a Rousseau-
like pristine state61. Such uninhibited freedom must
have seemed particularly appealing to Russians who
lived under austere autocratic control. Additionally
emphasizing his interest in Caucasian cultures and
peoples, Bestuzhev-Marlinsky learned Azeri, a Tatar
tongue, and even included tribal death songs expertly
rendered into Russian verse by the author and discussed
in one of his thirty-nine footnotes in his 1832 story,
Ammalat-Bek62. He even gave the work the subtitle
byl  (true story)63. In spite of these realist tendencies,
Bestuzhev-Marlinsky simultaneously portrayed the
conquest with a disparate kind to the travelogue, which
revitalized the cloying sentimentalist prose64.
Mikhail Iurevich Lermontov (1814-1841)
more aggressively criticized Russian imperial efforts.

His 1832 poem, Izmail-Bey, for instance, conveyed the
overwhelming atrocities committed in the Caucasus by
Russian military forces:
[w]here are the mountains, steppes and oceans/
[u]nconquered by the Slavs in war?/And where
have enmity and treason/[n]ot bowed to Russias
mighty Tsar?/Circassian, fight no more! Likely as
not,/[b]oth East and West will share your lot./The
time will come: youll say, quite bold,/I am a slave,
but my Tsar rules the world./The time will come:
the North will be graced/[b]y an awesome new
Rome a second Augustus./Aulsi are burning, their
defenders mastered,/[t]he homelands sons have
fallen in battle./Like steady comets, fearful to the
eyes,/[a] glow is playing cross the skies,/[a] beast
of prey with bayonet, the victor/[c]harges into a
quiet dwelling./ He kills the children and the old
folks,/[a]nd with his bloody hands he strokes/[t]he
unmarried girls and young mothers65.
Such disparaging depictions of action in Caucasia
effectively confronted Russian audiences with the
conquests sheer inhumanity.
In Izmail-Bey and later in his 1841 work, A
Hero of Our Time, Lermontov expressed his contempt
for blind romantic glorification of Caucasian military
campaigns. Mocking the anti-scientific, improbable
aspects of the romantic literary style, Lermontov
sarcastically announced his intentions to spare the
audience statistical remarks about the Caucasus
because he figured nobody would read them anyway66.
By challenging and ironically satirizing affected
romantic accounts of the conquests violent setting,
Lermontov affirmed alternatively a mode of realistic
literary transcription that made the reader reflect
personally and autonomously on the conquest.
By the time of the Crimean War (1854-56),
the fallibility of Russian military might seemed readily
obvious. In many ways, the positive discourse of
Caucasian victory sharply juxtaposed the depressing
dialogue of the Crimean defeat. The modernized
skirmishes of the Crimean War bore witness to some of
the deadliest fighting the world had yet to encounter.
Count Lev Nikolayevich Tolstoy recounts how Russian
forces suffered the brunt of these losses in his 1855 text,
Sevastopol Sketches. For example, [w]hen [Tolstoy]
left for Sevastopol on November 23rd, 1854, he
[describes] how 10, 0000 Russians had been slaughtered
by the enemy war machine, confirming the horrific
physiognomy of war relative to any societys tolerance
for violence67. Having also spent time in the Caucasus
himself, Tolstoy came to emphasize the consciousness
of the individual apart from his imperial, authoritarian

Maternal Factors and Childhood Health

Poor nutritional status during childhood has major effects on long-term health.
In the setting of rural Ghana, childhood malnutrition is prevalent, despite the fact
proper nutrition guidelines have been incorporated into intervention programs.
Thus, barriers may be preventing mothers from using their nutritional knowledge
to make healthy decisions in the household. This study assesses the prevalence
of malnutrition and the factors affecting it as seen in a sample of Ghanaian
women and their children aged 3-24 months (n=33). Anthropometric measurements were collected on the children and interviews were conducted with the
mothers. Analysis found that malnourished children were more likely to be the
offspring of mothers who were married (p=0.012) and lacked national health
insurance (p=0.176). Low maternal nutritional knowledge was not significantly
related to low child nutritional status (p=0.221), however a statistical trend was
visible. Because marital status was related to other variables including nutritional knowledge (p=0.040) and number of people in the home (p=0.201), it is
possible that relationships in the home are a barrier to childhood health. Efforts
to improve the home dynamics and increase the use of national health insurance may decrease the level of childhood malnutrition in this setting.
INTRODUCTION
or newborns, breastfeeding is a
major determinant of health because
of the beneficial nutritional and
immunological properties of breast
milk1. At six months, proper intro-
duction of complementary foods, as
recommended by the World Health
Organization (WHO), is critical to health. According
to the 2003 Demographic Health Survey data, 25%
of children under the age of five years in Ghana are
stunted, or malnurished2. High prevalence of mal-
nutrition indicates that there are barriers preventing
mothers from following WHO recommendations.
Thus, understanding barriers preventing compliance
with feeding recommendations has implications for
the improvement of policy and intervention programs
used globally. While past research has found child
nutritional status to be associated with maternal formal
education and socioeconomic status3, little research has
focused on factors affecting maternal compliance to
feeding recommendations.
Recent research has focused on the role of the
mother within the household, specifically her ability to
make decisions regarding household resources, child-
care, and health9. Her actions regarding aspects of child
NORTHWESTERN UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH JOURNAL
health - introduction and type of complementary foods,
perception and treatment of disease - directly affect
child health. Evidence shows that a mothers practical
knowledge about nutrition is associated with higher
nutritional status; yet, her ability to make health related
decisions and access to resources are not guaranteed,
adding another dimension9. Recent study examined
gender dynamics of household decision-making and
found that treatment-seeking behavior was influenced
by ownership of children, ability to control funds
to pay for treatment, norms in payment responsibil-
ity, and marital status10. Attainment of these qualities
may depend on other factors - formal education and
socioeconomic status. While these studies in West Africa
demonstrate the influential role mothers play in child
health, they do not address the ability of mothers to use
their nutritional knowledge. This study examines moth-
ers differences that create the range of nutritional status
among their children.
Feeding practices is a primary area of maternal
variation. WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding
for the first six months of life after which breast milk is
not sufficient source of nutrients. Complementary feed-
ing transitions a child to adult food. In many develop-
ing countries, these recommendations are not followed.
While mean duration of breastfeeding in Ghana is 23
RESEARCH
months, median duration of exclusive breastfeeding is
only 3.2 months2. The child does not like the breast or
likes food better are common reasons given as to why
exclusive breastfeeding was stopped. Further, comple-
mentary food typically provided is kooko, a thin, low
energy, low protein mixture. Children do not receive the
necessary nutrients for growth and immune function.
Unhealthy preparation, such as use of contaminated wa-
ter or addition of spices, causes further problems. Many
highly malnourished children are exposed to infection,
which exacerbates malnutrition. Thus, wasting is often
prevalent at one and two years of age, increasing the risk
of mortality4. Findings of this study would contribute to
knowledge of barriers to child health and have implica-
tions on nutrition policy and interventions.
Growth is an indicator of environmental and
social conditions affecting past, present, and future
health4 because it is sensitive to changes, adapting to
lack or excess of nutrients5. When infants receive inad-
equate nutrients, they lack energy, resulting in growth
retardation, which leads to stunting, an indicator for
chronic malnutrition6. Inadequate nutrients causes
protein energy malnutrition, which is detrimental to the
immune system. Slowing the speed of immunological
response puts risk on the child for infection and dis-
ease6. Nutritional studies on factors affecting malnutri-
tion have focused on effects of socioeconomic status,
maternal education, and birth order3,7,8. Although an
understanding of factors associated with child malnutri-
tion exists and used in intervention guidelines, malnu-
trition continues to be prevalent in developing coun-
tries. Thus, other factors may prevent the attainment of
higher nutritional status.
Ghana is in West Africa, just north of the equa-
tor, and situated on the Gulf of Guinea, with a popula-
tion of nearly 23 million, according to the World Bank.
Figure.
The country is divided into four regions. The Volta
Region is the south-eastern region that borders Togo.
Ho, the capital of the Volta Region, is the research site.
Ethnically, a majority of the inhabitants and Ewe and
speak Ewe, the indigenous language. The town has two
modern hospitals, numerous clinics, and several educa-
tion institutions. Study participants are from a range of
living backgrounds.
The aim of this study is to examine the rela-
tionship between mothers use of nutritional knowledge
and the effects on child growth. Associations between
maternal decision-making ability, nutritional knowl-
edge, and child nutritional status are examined in the
setting of rural Ghana. The three objectives are: describe
prevalence of stunting and wasting in the population,
examine its relationship with maternal nutritional
knowledge, and identify possible barriers to health
based on their relationship with nutritional status.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Study Population
This study uses data collected during a two-month field
study based in the Volta Region, Ghana.  The study
sample was recruited from the villages surrounding a
health center located in Voradep village, at the edge of
the Ho Municipal District. 34 mother-child pairs were
recruited, interviewed, and measured.  Recruitment
of participants was done by: (1) visitors to the center
during the study and (2) in villages near the center after
discussions with community leaders.  These sources
were used to ensure a random sample of mothers ac-
tively seeking treatment for their children and those that
are not.
Data Collection
The study collected anthropometric measurements of

determine the relationships between offspring growth
status and mothers nutritional knowledge. Data were
collected in interviews and were obtained under condi-

clearance from Northwestern University. Interviews
consisted of open and closed ended questions and
obtained information regarding demographic, home
structure, knowledge and perceptions of nutrition and
health, and role in the household.
Child anthropometrics were obtained using
standard techniques. Trained investigators weighed chil-
dren on a hanging scale to the nearest 0.1kg. Length was
measured to the nearest 0.1cm using an infant stadiom-
eter. To determine nutritional status, length-for-age,
weight-for-age, and weight-for-length were compared
to the WHO Child Growth Standards for appropriate
z-scores (WHO 2006). HAZ values below 2SD are
indicative of growth stunting or chronic malnutrition,
while WAZ values below 2SD demonstrate wasting or
acute malnutrition11.
Statistical Analysis
Nutritional status z-scores were obtained using ver-
sion 2 of the WHO Anthro software (World Health
Organization), with an anthropometric calculator. It
used the age of child - as determined from the date of
birth and date measured - length in centimeters, weight
NORTHWESTERN UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH JOURNAL
in kilograms, and gender to calculate the z-scores. All
statistical analyses were conducted using version 10 of
Stata (Stata Corporation, College Station, TX). Ma-
ternal Nutritional Knowledge was coded as an ordinal
variable with values ranging from 3 to 7. For analyses,
a new dichotomous high/low variable was generated (0
= nutritional knowledge of 3, 4, or 5; 1 = nutritional
knowledge of 6 or 7). Nutritional status was analyzed
as dichotomous variables. A series of chi-squared tests
were run to determine associations between nutritional
status variables, predictor variables and potential con-
founding variables. With this set of relationships, analy-
sis of health in the population is conducted. Analyses
were restricted to a subsample of mothers and children
for whom all tested variables were present (n= 33). One
pair was excluded because length could not be measured
accurately at the interview.

Although this was not expected, mothers may be unable

Table 5: NHIS: Chi-Squared p-values
With the set of chi-squared tests, it was found that
mothers possession of the National Health Insurance
Scheme (NHIS) affected child health. The Ghana Health
Services (GHS) instated the NHIS in 2003 with the goal
of achieving universal coverage12. Currently, the NHIS
costs 12 Ghana Cedi, which is the rough equivalent of
$12, per year. This covers outpatient costs (ie. dental
and eye-care) and most inpatient costs (ie. hospital
stays and medications). However, many people are not
members.  Only 56.7% of the sample had purchased the
health insurance.
The data shows that there are benefits of
NHIS on health. Stunted children were, on average, the
offspring of mothers who did not have NHIS (p=0.176).
RESEARCH
Also, mothers who possessed NHIS more frequently had
high nutritional knowledge (p=0.198) and used clean
water (p=0.070). Thus, nutritional knowledge may be
the base factor that leads to healthier actions, such
as a mothers possession of NHIS, use of clean water,
and feeding children nutritious complementary foods,
which positively affect nutritional status. These results
provide evidence for positive effects NHIS has on the
population and could motivate other mothers. Mothers
without NHIS frequently stated it was because they did
not have money, their husband did not want it, or she
did not know it was important.
DISCUSSION
Mothers with high nutritional knowledge were often
single, feeding their children nutrient-rich foods, and
in possession of NHIS. These findings were significant
and consistent with previous research. The expected
finding that mothers with high nutritional knowledge
would have children with high nutritional status, was
not significant, but rather showed a statistical trend.
However, Appoh et.al found that a mothers practical
knowledge about nutrition is associated with higher nu-
tritional status9. Thus, although this study did not find
significant relationships between nutritional knowledge
and nutritional status, an analysis of potential barriers
to health can still take place.  The main objectives of this
study were addressed. First, this population has signifi-
cant malnutrition based on the study sample, which is
important to identify specifically for the health center in
order to evaluate the progress of intervention programs.
In the total sample, 42% were stunted (LAZ<-2SD),
36% wasting (WAZ<-2SD), and 18% malnourished
(WLA<-2SD).
Second, analysis found low nutritional knowl-
edge weakly predicts low nutritional status. The scale
uses both actions and knowledge related to health.
Several factors were confirmed to be related to child
health outcome, including: providing colostrum at
birth and feeding proper complementary food. Mothers
lacking these factors more commonly had malnourished
children. This confirms that health-related actions cor-
respond to nutritional knowledge, as used by Appoh
et.al in the Maternal Nutritional Knowledge Scale9.
The final objective of this study examined
potential barriers to health. Marriage was related to low
nutritional status in her offspring, which is the opposite
of previous study by Appoh et.al in a similar popula-
tion9. Findings suggest the need for further research to
determine what factors are involved. Analysis showed
that single mothers also had higher nutritional knowl-
edge, which is also related to high nutritional status.
These results have important theoretical implications
for evaluating the role of kinship relations and house-
hold structure on child health. The income disparity
within the home may affect decision-making ability
and, in turn, child health. Fantahun et.al showed that
low maternal decision-making capacity and low socio-
economic status were associated with high under-five
mortality14, an outcome variable related to child health.
In this study, mothers with higher decision-making
ability were found to have less healthy children; how-
ever, structural barriers may be limiting her choices.
She may have to sell their entire groundnut, or peanut,
crop because it yields more money in the market even
though it is essential to the porridge mothers prepare
because of its protein content. When prepared with-
out groundnut, porridge contains only carbohydrates,
which could lead to malnutrition. Thus, it may be that
the mother is not making unhealthy choices, but that
her economic plight has limited her ability to make
healthy ones. Results have significant implications for
global health interventions. By identifying barriers to
health, it is possible to increase program effectiveness at
health centers. Programs should address female empow-
erment to allow mothers to use their knowledge to make
healthy decisions for their families.
The possession of NHIS was found to have
positive effects on nutritional status, which has implica-
tions on how the GHS campaigns to increase member-
ship. Factors, such as: access to care, socioeconomic
status, and acceptance of the program, are limiting.
Thus, the GHS must address these issues to reach their
goal of universal health care.
Small sample size is the major limitation
because of constraints it places on obtaining statisti-
cally significant p-values.  While significance was found,
many relationships demonstrated statistical trends.
The small sample size has ruled out logistic regres-
sion, which would allow more complex examination of
potential confounding variables.  Because mothers self-
reported their own actions taking place up to two years
in the past, error may have also occurred. A similar,
larger study is necessary to confirm the current findings.
Because several of the relationships may be related to
income inequality, further study should address socio-
economic status (SES).  SES may prevent a mother from
taking actions that promote her childrens health, such
as: nutritious complementary foods, adequate food,
NHIS, and clean water.  Further study should also take
place to better understand the dynamics of kinship rela-
tions. While this study collected responsibilities women
had in the household, it would be beneficial to gain a
better understanding of how they spent their time.
CONCLUSION
In rural Ghana, prevalence of child malnutrition is
related to feeding of nutrient poor complementary
NORTHWESTERN UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH JOURNAL
RESEARCH
foods, marriage, and lack of NHIS.  High nutritional
knowledge was more commonly seen in single mothers
and those with NHIS. Further study to examine these
dynamics will enhance the significant implications of
these findings. Anthropology will benefit from greater
understanding of pathways leading to desirable child
health while global health intervention programs could
be made more effective. Potential long-term effects of
marriage and nutritional knowledge on child health call
for immediate attention in research studies and global
health initiatives.

The goal of this research was to determine which modes, drive systems, and
fuels produce the lowest CO2 emissions per passenger-mile in urban passenger
transportation. Using Argonne National Laboratory’s GREET model as well as
real world fuel economy data, carbon dioxide emissions were determined for
each transportation pathway (combination of mode, drive system, and fuel). The
results show that the transit bus mode had slightly higher carbon dioxide emissions per passenger-mile than the automobile mode. The drive system results
show that hybrid drive systems and electric vehicles both offered a 30% reduction
in carbon dioxide emissions compared to vehicles that use conventional combustion engine technology. Plug-in hybrids released slightly more carbon dioxide
emissions than standard gasoline hybrids while hydrogen fuel cell emissions
were heavily dependent on the source of the hydrogen. Biofuels such as cellulosic
ethanol and B100 biodiesel had the lowest carbon dioxide emissions of any fuel.
The results provided a sense of what technologies offer the greatest reductions
in carbon dioxide emissions but this information should be used with caution.
Many other factors such as cost, system scalability, and consumer preference
play a critical role in the viability of each transportation pathway.
1. INTRODUCTION AND SCOPE
n recent years, policymakers have expressed
interest in finding ways to reduce greenhouse
gas (GHG) emissions since it is very likely
that these emissions contribute to global
warming (IPCC, 2007). Carbon dioxide
(CO2) is the most ubiquitous greenhouse gas
and was the focus of this research. In 2007,
the transportation sector of the US economy produced
2,014 million metric tons of carbon dioxide which is
approximately 1/3 of the US total production (EIA,
2008a). While the transportation sector encompasses
both freight and passenger transportation in both
urban and rural environments, only urban passenger
transportation was examined in this study. The goal
was to determine which modes, drive systems, and fuels
produce the lowest CO2 emissions per passenger-mile
traveled.
Two modes, seven drive systems, and ten fuels
were analyzed in various combinations to determine
their CO2 emissions. Each combination of mode, drive
system, and fuel is referred to as a transportation path-
way. For example, one pathway could be a transit bus
powered by an internal combustion engine that burns
diesel fuel.
1.1 Other Considerations
The results are not the product of a life cycle assess-
ment of urban passenger transportation since they are
limited to one output: carbon dioxide emissions. A life
cycle assessment of each vehicle pathway would have
accounted for many other inputs and outputs associated
with the system including cost, energy, fuel, and criteria
pollutants. Furthermore, a life cycle assessment would
account for the inputs and outputs from infrastructure
construction, vehicle manufacture, vehicle operation,
and vehicle disposal (Chester, 2008).
Other important considerations that were
ignored are system scalability and consumer preference.
Scalability is a measure of a systems ability to handle
growth. Consumer preference is a measure of how
much demand there is for a particular pathway. Both of
these factors are critical when assessing the viability of
each transportation pathway.
2. METHODOLOGY
Analysis of fuels using Argonne National Laboratorys
GREET model (ANL, 2008) as well as published fuel
economy data for a mix of vehicles allowed for the
computation of carbon dioxide emissions. The GREET
model accepts inputs such as fuel type and production
methods to create an output of CO2 and other emission
NORTHWESTERN UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH JOURNAL
RESEARCH
data for a hypothetical automobile. Part of the analy-
sis focused on commercially available vehicles which
are either currently in use or on the market. Real fuel
economy data was used for these vehicles. A number of
the vehicles analyzed are not commercially available or
lack sufficient data on fuel economy. For these vehicles,
GREET model estimates of fuel consumption were used.
Combining the relative efficiencies of the
vehicles with the carbon dioxide emissions of the fuels
provided the carbon dioxide emission per vehicle mile.
These values were then divided by average vehicle oc-
cupancies (number of passengers) to produce emissions
per passenger-mile.

portation such as rail, biking, and walking, the bus and
automobile were chosen because they share infrastruc-
ture such as roads and parking facilities. As a result,
infrastructure is a less important factor for comparison
purposes.

5.2 Petroleum Fuels
Gasoline and diesel are both petroleum fuels which
are derived from crude oil which is a non-renewable
resource. Most carbon dioxide production comes from
the consumption of these fuels, but fuel extraction,
Figure 1.
transportation, and refinery processes also produce
carbon dioxide.
5.3 Biofuels
The two biofuels analyzed were ethanol and biodiesel.
Biofuels are derived from biomaterials such as plant and
animal matter. Biodiesel is available in several blends,
two of which were analyzed here: B20 and B100. B100
is pure biodiesel and B20 is a more common blend of
biodiesel and includes 80% petroleum diesel and 20%
biodiesel. Biodiesels most common feedstock in the
US is soybean oil, however, it can be made from almost
any vegetable oil, animal fat, and algae. Only biodiesel
from soybeans was analyzed. Approximately 22% of
the soybean mass is vegetable oil, while the remaining
78% is soybean meal (Van Gerpen). The GREET model
gives a carbon dioxide emission credit for the soybean
meal co-product since it is used in animal feed and can
displace other sources of animal feed.
Ethanol is made from the fermentation and
distillation of biomass. Different blends of gasoline and
ethanol can be produced. The mixture analyzed was E85
ethanol which is a blend of 85% ethanol and 15% gaso-
line. There is disagreement among researchers about
CO2 emissions from ethanol production. The majority
of research indicates that corn ethanol has a net benefit

over gasoline in terms of CO2 emissions (NRDC, 2006).
Cellulosic ethanol can be made from any plant material
and uses the entire biomass of the plant whereas corn
ethanol only uses the biomass found in the corn kernels
(NRDC, 2006). The GREET model shows cellulosic
ethanol to be superior to corn based ethanol in terms
of CO2 emissions. The feedstocks in the model were
50% woody (tree) biomass and 50% herbaceous (grass)
biomass. One of the key advantages to cellulosic ethanol
production is that most processing plants burn lignin
in place of natural gas. Lignin is a component of the cell
wall of the plants that cannot be converted into ethanol.
5.4 Natural Gas
Natural gas is composed primarily of methane gas
and is part of the fossil fuel family. Figure 1 shows that
combustion of natural gas yields slightly lower carbon
dioxide emissions per MJ of energy than combustion of
diesel or gasoline since it has lower carbon to hydrogen
ratio.
5.5 Hydrogen
Hydrogen gas can be made from a variety of sources
but the two most common feedstocks are electricity and
natural gas. Hydrogen is made from electricity through
the electrolysis process which is about 60-70% efficient
(Ivy, 2004). The CO2 emissions of electrolyzed hydrogen
are dependent on the source of the electricity. Figure 1
shows that hydrogen made from the current US electric-
ity mix has the highest CO2 emissions per MJ of the
ten fuels. Nevertheless, hydrogen from electrolysis has
great potential to reduce CO2 emissions if the electricity
comes from renewable sources such as wind and solar.
Hydrogen can also be obtained from natural
Figure 2.
gas through a reforming process in which the hydrogen
is stripped from the methane molecules. 95% of the hy-
drogen produced in the US comes from steam reformed
methane (DOE, 2008b). The process releases carbon
dioxide and requires a significant energy input since the
reactions take place at 700-1000 degrees Celsius at 3-25
bars of pressure (EERE, 2008b).
5.6 Electricity
Electricity can be used directly as a fuel and it is also a
feedstock for the other fuels discussed. Figure 2 shows
the feedstock mix for US electricity. This mix was taken
from the GREET model as an estimate for the year 2010
but matches closely to the feedstock mix published by
the US Department of Energy for the year 2006 (EIA,
Figure 1 demonstrates that electricity has the
second highest CO2 emissions per MJ compared to
the other eight fuels. Obviously, changing the electric-
ity mix in the US to include more renewable sources
and less coal will change the carbon dioxide profile of
electricity. In addition, carbon sequestration technolo-
gies employed at coal fired power plants could also have
a positive impact on the CO2 emissions of electricity.
