Several models of transit bus were used from
each transit agency (CTA and NYCT). For the CTA,
these included fleet averages for buses with internal
combustion engines, hybrid drives, as well as the New

6.1 Transit Bus Results
The CTA fleet appears to have lower CO2 emissions
than the NYCT buses but this is likely attributable to the
fact that the CTA data came from newer vehicles. The
difference could also be attributable to the geography
of each city. The results also show that hybrid drives
and biodiesel offered significantly lower carbon dioxide
emissions than internal combustion engines and diesel
respectively. Finally, Figure 3 shows the significant car-
bon dioxide emission reductions that can be achieved
by increasing vehicle occupancy in buses.
6.2 Automobile Results
The results show that the transit buses tend to have
higher CO2 emissions per passenger-mile than the cars
for average occupancy levels. Part of this difference is
attributable to the manner in which the fuel economy
data was collected for each mode. The age of the vehi-
cles may also play a role since the bus data was collected
from older vehicles than the car data. However, the CO2
emissions of the CTAs 2008 diesel lightweight bus were
higher than those of every car model except for the
gasoline powered Tahoe indicating that vehicle age may
not be a significant factor.
The results also show that the spark ignition
(SI) internal combustion engine was one of the highest
emitters of CO2 regardless of whether gasoline or natu-
ral gas was used as the fuel. CIDI diesel engines offered
a reduction in carbon dioxide emissions of about 20%
compared with SI engines. Use of a hybrid-electric drive
system reduced emission approximately 30% when
compared to vehicles that only use an internal com-
bustion engine. Cellulosic ethanol and B100 biodiesel
produced the least CO2 emissions of any fuel.

The results for the non-commercially available vehicles
were obtained directly from the GREET model since
real fuel consumption data was not available. The hypo-

8. CONCLUSIONS
The results of this study provide information about
which transportation pathways produce the least carbon
dioxide per passenger-mile traveled. Such information
is useful when selecting modes, vehicles, and fuels with
NORTHWESTERN UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH JOURNAL
the goal of reducing carbon dioxide emissions. Further-
more, it provides information to policy-makers about
which technologies currently offer the most promise in
terms of immediate investment. Several fuels and drive
systems stood out as offering a clear carbon dioxide
reduction over traditional petroleum fuels and inter-
nal combustion engines respectively and merit further
study. Biodiesel and cellulosic ethanol fall into this
category since these two fuels had the lowest emissions
per unit of energy. For drive systems, hybrids and CIDI
RESEARCH
engines offer clear benefits over SI internal combus-
tion engines and these technologies are already making
significant headway in the marketplace. In addition to
carbon emissions, policymakers and investors will need
to take other factors into consideration such as cost,
scalability, consumer preference, and technical barriers
to mainstream production when evaluating each trans-
portation pathway.
8.1 Further Study
Since fuel cell vehicles, plug-in hybrids, and electric
vehicles are not yet commercially available, it is unfair
to discount them until more data can be collected. As
these technologies develop over the next decade, further
comparisons to internal combustion engines should be
made. In addition, better information on vehicle occu-
pancy should be obtained for transit buses, particularly
with regard to low occupancy and maximum occupancy
conditions. A distribution of transit bus occupancy
levels throughout its route would be helpful rather than
relying on a national average occupancy level.
The next step to analyzing the transportation
pathways is to account for other factors in addition to
net operating CO2 emissions. Ultimately, a life cycle
analysis of each of the vehicle pathways should be per-
formed that includes all inputs and outputs of pathway
components. Only then will investors have all of the
information they need to make intelligent decisions
about urban transportation pathways.

Community Organization and Family Strength
in Watts on the Eve of the 1965 Rebellion
Colin McGrath
DEPARTMENT OF HISTORY
Henry Binford
FACULTY ADVISOR
DEPARTMENT OF HISTORY
NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY
O
n August 11th, 1965, one of the largest urban
uprisings in American history broke out in
Los Angeles.i Black residents from the Watts
district  and  surrounding  areas  looted  local
businesses,  burned  buildings,  overturned  cars,  fought
police officers, and stoned firemen. The district and its
surrounding areas contained a concentrated population
of  black  Americans  who  suffered  from  acute  poverty.
During  the  rebellion,  reporters  depicted  images  of
hoodlums  running  lawless  through  the  streets  of  Los
Angeles. All major newspapers termed the conflagration
a  riot.  Professional-class  Americans  argued  that  the
rebellion erupted in a community where poor leadership
and broken homes produced a riot-prone youth. Yet the
black community evinced substantive forms of political
and social organization at the time of the rebellion. Blacks
developed organizational tools to cope with their shared
experience of poverty and discrimination. The rebellions
pattern  of  property  damage  shows  that  participants
targeted the same set of structural injustices. They were
integrated  within  an  organized  and  politically  engaged
community. Urban violence was the black communitys
response  to  political,  social,  and  economic  inequalities
NORTHWESTERN UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH JOURNAL
the  U.S.s  racialized  political  economy  produced.  For
participants,  the  conflagration  offered  the  only  means
for expressing outrage; political marginalization denied
black  residents  any  other  effective  avenues.ii    But
professional-class  Americans  failed  to  seeand  chose
to ignorethe political intent of the black community.
Contemporaneous  social  science  research  influenced
professional-class  perceptions  of  poverty  and  distorted
their interpretation of the rebellion.
Culture of Poverty, Tangle of Pathology
In the 1960s, social scientists in the United States produced
a  body  of  research  highlighting  cultural  differences
between  poor  and  affluent  Americans.  Researchers
among them Oscar Lewis, Daniel Patrick Moynihan, and
Kenneth Clarkinvestigated the cultural pathologies of
poor communities to explain the production of poverty
across  generations.  By  synecdoche,  anthropologist
Oscar  Lewis  applied  the  conclusions  from  his  popular
ethnography on Latin American poverty to the poverty
of black Americans.iii In 1963 he wrote an article, The
Culture of Poverty, in which he claimed, The problems
we think of as distinctivelyNegro problems also exist
in countries where there are no ethnic groups involved.iv
He explained that culture, not racial conflict, perpetuated
poverty in the U.S. In 1965, psychologist Kenneth Clark
published Dark Ghetto and described urban poverty thus:
The ghetto develops the sinister power to perpetuate its
own  pathology,  to  demand  conformity  to  its  norms.v
He coined a term, tangle of pathology, to encapsulate
the  debilitating  cultural  he  found  endemic  in  poor
communities.
Sociologist  and  politician  Daniel  Patrick
MoynihanAssistant  Secretary  of  Labor  and  Director
of Policy Planning and Research under the Kennedy and
Johnson administrationsborrowed Clarks term in his
study  The  Negro  Family:  The  Case  for  National  Action,
popularly  titled,  The  Moynihan  Report.  The  study
explained that the insidious tangle of pathology ensnared
black youths. Central to the tangle, he explained, was the
weakness  of  the  family  structure.vi  Through  slavery
and  subsequent  penury,  black  men  lost  the  masculine
traits  necessary  for  raising  successful  families.  Without
suitable fathers, children flounder and failvii: they grow
up lacking ambition and are unable to successfully raise
their own children. Moynihan concluded that the tangle
of pathology could perpetuate itself without assistance
from  the  white  world.viii  His  reasoning  echoed  that  of
Oscar  Lewis:  racial  injustice  could  no  longer  explain
inequality  in  the  United  States.  The  ghetto  produced
poverty on its own.
Government  officials  intended  for  the  Moynihan
Report to remain an internal document. But in July 1965
full summaries of the report leaked into the public sphere
and fomented a nationwide debate on race, poverty, and
the  structure  of  black  families.  When  the  rebellion  in
Watts broke out a month later, the Moynihan Report was
the primary frame of reference through which Americans
interpreted the conditions in Watts and the meaning of
the rebellion.
As  journalists  and  government  officials  struggled
to understand the rebellion, they failed to recognize the
rebellions  social  and  political  impetus.  Through  the
lens  of  racial  stereotypes  and  literature  on  the  culture
of  poverty,  whitesand  some  blacksdeemed  the
rebellion  a  meaningless  riot:  it  was  the  product  of
pathologies  social  scientists  found  endemic  in  black
urban  ghettos.  Journalists  reported  that  community
disorganization,  emasculation  and  shiftlessness  of
black males, and single-mother households destabilized
black  neighborhoods.  A  headline  in  the  Wall  Street
Journal  boldly  announced,  Behind  the  Riots:  Family
Life  Breakdown  in  Negro  Slums  Sows  Seeds  of  Race
Violence. The article argued that the violence was not
protesting  any  specific  civil  rights  grievances.  Instead,
the  participants  were  primarily  young  hoodlums
lashing out against society and authority in general. Such
RESEARCH
youths, it added, are being bred in the Negro sections of
cities across the country by broken homes, illegitimacy,
and  other  social  ills.ix  Other  journalism  explicitly
referenced  the  Moynihan  Report.  On  August  26th,  the
Chicago Tribune proclaimed, Study Traces Negro Riots
to Inferior Homes.x Rowland Evans and Robert Novaks
column  The  Inside  Report  drew  another  explicit  link
between Watts and Moynihan. In a brief summary of the
Moynihan  Report,  they  asserted  that  key  White  House
figures  feel  that  the  Moynihan  report  might  open  the
door to new ideas and avert continuous guerrilla warfare
in Negro ghettoes.xi
The McCone Commissiona research group that
Californias  Governor  Brown  appointed  to  investigate
the  rebellionechoed  these  views  in  an  official  report
titled,  Violence  in  the  CityAn  End  or  a  Beginning?  xii
But  the  commissions  own  records  reveal  a  different
image of the community. Their interviews with residents
of  Watts  show  that  members  of  the  community  were
more  articulate,  organized,  and  perspicacious  than
professional-class Americans reported.
Coping Mechanisms and Forms of Social
Organization in Watts
Individuals in Watts took proactive actions to cope with
their adverse circumstances. Unemployed black men did
not constitute a uniformly weak and depressed segment
of society; men found informal yet legal ways to secure an
income. Single mothers took proactive steps to organize
with one another in order to care for their children and
navigate  bureaucratic  mazes  to  access  welfare  money.
Youths  in  Watts  formed  political  coalitions  to  combat
social  and  economic  injustices  within  the  community.
These interlocking actions held Watts together while Los
Angeless white-dominated society threatened to break it
apart.
Because  white  employers  were  reluctant  to  hire
blacks,  men  in  Watts  became  informal  entrepreneurs.
Their  entrepreneurship  mitigated  the  neighborhoods
chronic unemployment. One man named Willie Brown
described  himself  as  professionally  unemployed.xiii
To  secure  an  income  for  himself  while  assisting  men
in  situations  similar  to  his  own,  Brown  established
an  informal  employment  and  transportation  service.
Individuals from Woodland Hills, a more affluent city in
the San Fernando Valley, had provided Brown with a 37-
seat bus. He used the bus to transport day laborers from
Watts  to  Woodland  Hills  for  work  that  paid  $14  a  day.
Each worker paid Brown $2 a day for his service.
Young-adults  in  Watts  formed  organizations  to
strengthen  their  communitys  bonds  and  ameliorate
their living conditions. Students at Jordan High School,
a  low-income  school  in  Watts,  founded  one  such
organization: the Student Committee for Improvement

RESEARCH
in  Watts  (SCFIW),  which  had  120  registered  members
and 80 active participants.xiv The SCFIW addressed many
of the problems of economic exploitation and absentee
ownership that the rebellion would later target through
violence. The group petitioned against absentee landlords
who allowed buildings to deteriorate. Lynda Bryant, the
SCFIWs president, inveighed against poor ownership
and observed: The people who owned the buildings had
left  and  they  didnt  care  about  the  buildings,  orhow
they were kept up. The group gathered 2,500 signatures
in  opposition  to  property  neglect  and  successfully
campaigned to convert the abandoned and deteriorating
Villa Maria Hotel into a community cultural center.xv The
SCFIW also assisted in a campaign to register voters in
opposition to Californias Proposition 14, legislation that
would allow landholders to deny property sales to buyers
on the basis of race.xvi Two SCFIW members received a
grant from UCLAs Industrial Relations Department to
publish  a  research  paper  in  the  research  compilation,
Hardcore  Unemployment  and  Poverty  in  Los  Angeles.xvii
Students  in  Watts  cared  about  their  surroundings  and
could successfully mobilize their community to combat
sources of exploitation and urban decay.
Voices from Watts
Following  the  rebellion,  the  McCone  Commission
hired investigators to interview individuals from Watts.
Through listening to the black communitys grievances,
the commission hoped to ascertain the rebellions causes.
Concerns that blacks articulated corresponded with the
frustrations that inspired blacks from Watts to engage in
social  and  economic  entrepreneurship.  These  concerns
also paralleled the injustices participants in the rebellion
reacted  to  with  violence.  Frequent  themes  included
employers racist hiring patterns, antagonistic community-
police relations, white shopkeepers exploitation of black
customers, and political marginalization.
Blacks from  Watts linked chronic unemployment
to  employers  racist  hiring  practices  and  Los  Angeless
racialized, segregated industrial geography. At the Avalon
Community  Center  near  Watts,  blacks  who  attended  a
meeting  with  a  government  investigator  observed  that
the  stores  in  the  area  refused  to  hire  minorities,  and
especially Negroes.xviii A younger girl stated, When you
go  to  look  for  a  job,  they  dont  want  you.xix  The  jobs
blacks did get were so marginal that the employers go
out  of  business  or  go  bankrupt  before  they  are  able  to
pay them. Some employers refused to pay their workers.
xx
One man recounted having excelled in school only to
graduate and not find a job because employers favored
whites: I was a better student than them, but they got
the jobs. Even if the citys hiring and firing process was
legally  fair,  he  observed,  It  doesnt  stop  the  individual
from  practicing  discrimination.xxi  Others  noted  that
NORTHWESTERN UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH JOURNAL
the stable, well-paying jobs were situated far outside of
Watts.
In  Watts  and  nearby  areas,  police  officers
symbolized  the  white  power  structure  that  oppressed
black  Americans.  One  resident  stated,  The  people  in
Watts call the police the Gestapochildren and adults
alike.xxii A woman claimed that the police would request
sexual favors. If a woman refused to comply, she would
go  to  jail  on  some  trumped-up  charge.  The  police
would  hold  unyielding  women  for  24  hours  before
releasing them without formal charges.xxiii A young man
named Doe participated in the rebellion because he had
a  personal  dislike  for  the  police  ever  since  two  white
officers  attempted  to  rape  his mother.xxiv  In  a public
forum, a speaker linked his anger towards the police with
the  problem  of  unemployment  in  Watts.  He  observed,
If  two  or  moreboys  are  together,  they  are  always
picked up by the police and held for 24 hours. The police
would  release  them  without  pressing  any  charges,  but
the  youths  would  still  have  a  police  record,  and  when
they  apply  for  a  jobthey  are  denied  work.xxv  Watts
residents frequently and angrily quoted the Los Angeles
Police Departments Chief Parker as saying, Theyre like
a bunch of monkeys in a cage. To many blacks, Parkers
incautious, inflammatory comment confirmed the police
departments distain for the community.
In  many  discussions,  blacks  excoriated  white
business  ownersmany  of  whom  were  Jewishfor
exploiting blacks. A public-forum speaker stated that the
food  sold  in  his  neighborhood  was  exorbitantly  priced
and of inferior quality: the vegetables, the meat, and the
bread were almost always old and barely fit for human
consumption. Prices were higher in Watts than in white
neighborhoods  where  products  were  of  better  quality.
xxvi
Multiple  speakers  shared  in  this  frustration.  As  one
interviewee  vituperated:  There  were  just  a  bunch  of
Jews selling us a second-class merchandise for first-class
prices.xxvii
Patterns of Destruction
The pattern of property damage from the rebellion indi-
cates that participants acted in precise and consistent
ways that reflected the attitudes blacks shared through-
out the community. Participants burned and looted
stores owned by whitesespecially stores notorious for
selling inferior goods at exorbitant prices. They spared
homes, schools, community centers, black-owned busi-
nesses, and white-owned businesses with good reputa-
tions.
Though  no  leader  organized  the  Watts  rebellion,
a  logic  guided  the  pattern  of  property  destruction.  A
McCone Commission memorandum reported:
It  was  noted  that  the  burning  was
highly  selective.  The  Urban  Leagues,
Poverty  Program  Watts  Project,
for  example,  was  the  only  unburned
building  left  in  the  block.  A  Negro
owned  restaurant  was  left  standing
and  unlooted  while  a  furniture  store
next door was burned to the ground.
The memorandum also noted that some white businesses
were still operating and had not been bothered because:
they treated the people o.k. and did come back and open
their stores even after the newspapers and T.V. said this
was a race riot.  Further indicating  that the rebellions
logic  was  nuanced  enough  to  see  past  simple  racial
divisions,  the  memorandum  observed:  Some  Negro
businesses  (with  bad  policies  towards  customers)  were
attacked.xxviii
These  patterns  show  that  the  rebellions
participants  shared  their  perceived  injustices  with  the
rest  of  the  community.  Lynda  Bryant,  president  of  the
SCFIW, illustrated a bond between organized individuals
and the rebellions participants when she testified before
the McCone Commission. She linked the rebellion to the
frigid  business-community  relationship  in  Watts.  As  a
student who organized against economic injustice in her
community,  she  assailed  local  merchants  for  exploiting
their  customers.  In  Watts,  she  explained,  most  of  the
clothes  are  real  cheap,  the  material  and  allbut  the
prices  are  real  high.  In  her  opinion,  this  was  one  of
the  reasons  why  participants  burned  and  looted  stores
during  the  rebellion.xxix  Bryant  did  not  participate  in
the  conflagration.  She  nonetheless  saw  that  individuals
who resorted to violence did so for the same reasons that
inspired her involvement with the SCFIW.
Conclusion
The participants were engaged with the civic and
social life of their surrounding community. They
razed the businesses that exploited them and they
acted deliberately enough to preserve the agencies that
supported their community. Their actions stemmed
directly from the communitys underrepresentation
in Los Angeless political sphere: if civic politics
allowed blacks to pressure the city government into
policymaking beneficial to the Watts district, they
would not have resorted to political violence as a means
of expression.
Yet the McCone Commission blatantly ignored
this evidence in their report on the rebellion. In
so doing, they exonerated political leaders whose
favoritism and policymaking had facilitated Los
Angeless racial inequalities; they sanctioned the Los
Angeles Police Departments heavy-handed presence

in Watts; and they obviated the need to consider racist
attitudes among whites as a cause for the rebellion.
When professional-class Americans investigated and
reported on the Watts community, they chose to see
hoodlums rather than activists and pathology instead
of political intent. Echoing the tangle of pathology,
the McCone Commission evoked an ominous spiral
of failure when explaining the origins of the rebellion.
The commission warned that unemployed fathers
had compromised the stability of families, thereby
producing a riot-prone youth. Even if an unemployed
father remained with his family, such a man was
not a worthy example to his children. Unable to
motivate his children to succeed in school and life,
the unemployed parent passed his pathologies on to a
younger generation.xxx
This interpretation of the rebellion discursively
marginalized Los Angeless urban poor. It safeguarded
the socioeconomic status of American elites vis-à-vis
poor blacks after the rebellion brought a social order
into question. But the rebellions pattern of destruction
indicates that the violence was political, intentional,
and reflected the social and civic awareness of its
participants. It was not the passive product of social
pathologies among black youths. Individuals who
participated in the rebellion responded to the same
grievances that formal and informal organizations in
Watts worked to ameliorate. Only they did so with
a different method: violence. The rebellion was a
political tool for breaking down the racialized social and
economic forces that marginalized their community and
reproduced poverty across generations.

The ovarian follicle, the functional unit of the ovary, consists
of an oocyte surrounded by somatic granulosa cells. Women
(and mice) are born with a non-renewable follicle reserve, so
understanding how an individual follicle begins the process
of development during one menstrual cycle is crucial to the
progress of fertility research.[1] The mouse serves as an accurate
model of human follicle growth and development. It was
previously observed that the number of follicles during each
developmental stage depended on the strain of the mouse
tested.[2] Because the number of follicles differs among strains
of mice, we hypothesized that the expression of various genes
that control the follicle initiation stages must also differ between
mice strains. The gene expression patterns in pre-pubertal CD-1
and C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca mice ovaries were analyzed to determine
if they affected the very first follicle initiation stage. RNA was
isolated from ovarian samples (day 12 and 16) gene expression
levels of Gdf9, Bmp15, Fshr, Foxl2, Cyp11a, Cyp17, and Amh in the
ovary were determined through real-time PCR. The expression
levels of the Foxl2, Cyp11a and Cyp17 genes were found to vary
between day 12 and 16 in both strains of mice.
Introduction
Mice are commonly used as model systems for mam-
malian research, because they share a high degree of
anatomy and physiology with humans, including their
reproductive axis. Because women (and mice) are born
with a non-renewable number of follicles, understand-
ing how an individual follicle begins the process of
development during any given ovulatory cycle is a key
element to the progress of oncofertility.[1]
CD-1  and  C57BL/6j  x  CBA/Ca  are  two  mouse
strains used in our lab for follicle development studies. In
our present study, we focused on the pre-pubertal stage
of ovarian development in which the ovary has started
the early stages of follicular growth (folliculogenesis) in
preparation for the first ovulation. Here, we analyzed the
difference  in  follicle  development  between  two  strains
of mouse, inbred C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca and outbred CD-
1, and have identified key genes that may be important
in  the  regulation  of  early  follicle  development  in  both
strains and for the model, overall.
Materials and Methods
Animals
Female F1 of hybrids (C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca) and CD-
1 mice were bred in our lab. Mice were maintained
in accordance to all required policies. Breeding mice
were housed in constant temperature, humidity and
photoperiod (12L, 12D) with food and water available
ad libitum. Breeders (90-180d, 6-8 weeks old) were
fed with a soy-free mouse chow (Harlan 7926) to limit
exogenous phytoestrogen intake through food. At the
time of delivery (day of birth), eight pups were kept
with each female to minimize the possible difference in
pup development caused by nutrient availability.

RNA isolation and real-time PCR
Total RNA was isolated from ovaries (n=4) using a
Qiagen mini prep RNA isolation kit (Qiagen, Valencia,
CA) according to a manufacturer protocol. On-column
DNAse digestion was performed using an RNase-free
DNAse set (Qiagen) to eliminate DNA contamination.
1 µg of RNA of each sample was reverse transcribed
with MMV reverse transcriptase (Promega). Real-time
PCR was performed to reveal the expression of growth
differentiation factor 9 (GDF9), bone morphogenetic
protein 15 (BMP15), follicle stimulating hormone
receptor (FSHR), forkhead box L2 (FOXL2), CYP11A,
CYP17, and anti-müllerian hormone (AMH).
Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH)
served as an endogenous control.  PCR was performed
using Taqman gene expression assay according to
manufacturers instructions (Applied Biosystem).
Tissue processing and follicle counting
Animal ovaries were fixed overnight in 4%
paraformaldehyde and dehydrated before paraffin
embedding.  Serial sections of 5 µm were stained with
Hematoxylin and Eosin. The numbers of primordial,
primary, two-layer secondary and multi-layered
secondary follicles were examined under light-
microscope at 120X. The follicle counts and calculations
were performed according to a method developed
by the lab and used extensively to characterize
folliculogenesis.[3]
In vivo ovulation (IVO)
IVO was induced on postnatal day 21 in CD-1 and
C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca mice. The mice were injected i.p.
with 5 IU PMSG and then induced to ovulate with 5
IU hCG after 48 h. Intact cumulus-oocyte complexes
(COCs) were collected from the thin walled portion
of the oviduct 14 hours after hCG treatment under
the dissection microscope. The number of COCs was
counted.

Oocyte diameter measurement
The diameter of the oocytes of different stage follicles
and the oocytes acquired from COCs were measured
using SPOT Advanced software. The oocytes only
with obvious nucleolus were chosen for diameter
measurements.  The maximal distance across the oocyte

Statistical analysis
Comparisons for follicle counts, litter size, number
of COCs ovulated, oocyte diameter, hormone level,
and gene expression were made between CD-1 and

The expression of early folliculogenesis related genes
To further explore the mechanisms underlying the
differences in follicle development between two
strains of mice, genes known to be expressed in early
follicles were measured (Figure 3). Foxl2 (forkhead
box L2), Amh (anti-müllerian hormone), Gdf9
(growth differentiation factor 9), and Bmp15 (bone
morphogenetic protein 15) are important for early
stage follicle initiation and development.[4]  Fshr (follicle
stimulating hormone receptor) is critical for the
developing follicle in that it is the binding site of FSH.[5]
Cyp11a encodes the cholesterol side-chain cleavage
enzyme (P450scc) that catalyzes the first rate-limiting
step for the biosynthesis of sex hormones, and Cyp17
plays a critical role in the production of androgens.[6]

Discussion
In the present study, the regulation of follicle
development during the first stage of follicle initiation
(folliculogenesis) was examined in two strains of mice.
We determined that CD-1 mice have more primordial,
secondary, and total follicles after the initiation of
folliculogenesis than C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca mice have. In
addition, CD-1 mice have oocytes that are significantly
larger than those of C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca mice.  Even
though CD-1 mice have quantitatively more follicles,
oocyte development is identical in both strains. By
examining the follicle numbers in each strain, we
demonstrated the possible relation between follicle
development and the fertility of the animal. This
permits us to examine genes that are involved in follicle
development and not in oocyte health. We hypothesized
that since the follicle numbers differ between these
two strains, the expression of various genes that
control the follicle initiation stages would also differ.
Our hypothesis was proven by the results of our
experiments.  Higher levels of Foxl2 and Cyp11a were
expressed in CD-1 mice than in C57BL/6j x CBA/Ca
mice.  However, the levels of expression of Cyp17 were
lower in CD-1 mice than in C57 x CBA mice. It is now
crucial to understand how these genes regulate follicle
activation.  Importantly, these studies provide the first
window into early follicle activation and may be useful
to women who need to preserve their reproductive
potential at the time of cancer diagnosis.  The genes
identified here may serve as important markers of
healthy human follicle development in vitro.  From our
results, future work involving the relationship between
the number of COCs present in a mouse, the size of
a mouses litter, and the number of follicles a mouse
possesses may be explored.

Introduction
In this paper I intend to make a comparative analysis of
Velimir Khlebnikovs poems Venus and the Shaman
and Stone Woman, Natalia Goncharovas paint-
ings Planting Potatoes and Stone Woman, and Mikhail
Larionovs painting Jewish Venus.
In the first decade of the 20th century, leaders of
the emerging Russian avant-garde movement, Mikhail
Larionov, Natalia Goncharova, and Velimir Khlebnikov
made a conscious and deliberate decision to shake
off the tethers of Western European influence2 and
create art and poetry that is
uniquely Russian. They de-
fined this new Russianness
as Neoprimitivism. In their
quest for a national self-iden-
tity, they combined modern
literary and visual techniques
with primitive subject mat-
ter: peasants, soldiers, and
mythical figures from Russian
history and folklore. Through
the platform of Neoprimi-
tivsm, they proposed a model
of a future that is informed
and strengthened by the values and history of a unique-
ly Russian past.
I argue that Larinovs, Goncharovas, and Khleb-
nikovs representation of the cultural hero as a female
figure serves as a proposal for a future oriented toward
strong national self-identity, independent of Eurocen-
tric influence. This paper will also attempt to explain
why the female figure seemed to serve the nationalist
objectives of Neoprimitivism by embodying physical
and spiritual strength. My argument will proceed in
three parts. First, I will briefly outline the development
and goals of Neoprimitivism. I will then focus on the
representation of the female figure by offering close
readings of specific works of art and poetry. In conclu-
sion, I will discuss the stakes of my project.

highly nationalist.3 Enamored by progress, the Ital-
ian Futurists rejected the past. For instance, Marinetti
claimed that Progressis always right even when it
is wrong, because it is movement, life, struggle, hope
(Nicholls 99). According to the tenets of Italian Futur-

When Christian missionaries converted the Slavic
people, they could not subdue the pagan cult of the
Mother Goddess. Instead, they used the figure of Mary,
the Mother of God, as a replacement of Mokosh. While
in the West the virginity of Mary was stressed, in the
Russian Orthodox tradition it is her role as mother that
is most important (Hubbs 100). The following proverb
summarizes the attempts of the Christian missionaries
to eradicate the worship of Mother Earth: Your first
mother is Mary; your second mother is the earth; and
your third mother is your own mother (Hubbs 21).
Today, the country itself is still referred to as Mother
Russia.
It is important to recognize that the female is
more than just a symbol of fertility. Because of her
connection with land and nature, the woman is also
associated with physical and spiritual strength. In Rus-
sian tradition, just like nature is beyond human control,
there is something authentic, almost primal about
female strength that resists control by man, civiliza-
tion, domestication, or machinery. Even linguistically,
the words for nature, earth, planet, culture, homeland,
strength, freedom, independence, life, and Russia are all
female gendered words.
Russian Futurists wanted to build national iden-
tity by tapping into internal Russian traits and values
rather than by relying on external sources such as ma-
chinery and technology. The female, and their represen-
tation of her as a cultural hero, allowed the Futurists to
express these goals. Not only is the woman the mother
from whom Russian culture and history emanate, but
this image of the woman demonstrates strength and free
spiritedness that could defy the pressures of Westerniza-
tion and facilitate the construction of an independent
national identity. The exploration of the various degrees
and layers of strength embodied in the female figure
unifies the widely ranging Futurist works that focus on
the female form.
Khlebnikovs 1912 poem, Venus and the Sha-
man is a playful work in which the female figures
strong and willful sprit are represented through the
wanton, unbridled sexuality of the goddess Venus.12
Khlebnikov depicts Venus as fully nude, flirtatious, and
arrogant calling herself a river of delights. Her explo-
sive sexuality overflows bursting forth like spring fever
/ all in flower with the sultriness of passion gleaming
in her eyes. Permeating through her core, Venus sexual-
ity is so innate and deeply embedded in the essence of
her being, that it cannot be restrained even by Venus
herself. She finds herself in a dilemma because of her
inability to contain her sexuality and societys desire to
do just that.

Venuss worshipers abandon her because they
are unable to control her eroticism. Gradually turning
from polytheism, her followers become more conserva-
tive and try to civilize the goddess by forcing her to
conceal her nudity. They made me cover my forget-
me-nots!...Id rather die / than have to sunbathe on the
sly, complains a distraught Venus. Now, no one builds
statues in her honor, no one sings her praises, her name
has been forgotten, and her breasts, which used to con-
quer multitudes, are ignored.
Desperate and dejected, Venus seeks shelter
with the wise Shaman who has spent his life isolated
from society and civilization. In her vulnerable state
of abandonment, Venus seems to give into the pres-
sures to overcome her nature and accept domestication.
She claims that she wants to lead a simple life like the
Shaman and get back in touch with the birds and bees
/ far from the hum of the pressing crowd. Exerting a
genuine effort, she seems to grow more modest and self-
conscious. She blushes and questions whether it is polite
to show up naked in a strange mans house. When the
Shaman throws her a fox-fur jacket she does not resist
and is actually grateful for the cover. Venus even seems
to become more attune to housework as she crossly
chastises the Shaman, instructing him to keep his
dugout clean and to stop smoking! She also cuts open
the carcass of a deer and prepares one of her favorite
dishes: Venison a la Venus.
But the domestication and transformation of the
goddess of love into an irritable housewife is meant hu-
morously and satirically. Where did she learn to cook?
Olympus? It is a commentary on the process of domes-
tication and suggests that there is something unnatural
about external influences forcibly imposing changes on
ones character and impulses. Because it is unnatural,
Venus transformation is unsustainable and she doesnt
revel in the simple life of housewifery too long. A
dying swan delivers a message that her people love and
miss her and need her to return. Venus quickly decides
to leave the Shaman and asks him to forget my breasts.
/ Put them out of your mind. / Forget my face, my sweet
behind. Simple life is not for her. Instantly, Venus
reverts back to what she was when she first came to the
Shaman: untamed and uncovered sexuality. She strokes
his beard and disappears like a sweet mistake.
Venuss journey comes full circle and she embrac-
es the sexuality that caused her such grief. Though the
simplicity of her life with the Shaman may have been
tempting, even enjoyable, it was inorganic to her nature.
And just like Venus eventually shakes off her domes-
tication because it is alien to who she is, the Futurists
proposed that Russians shake off  the foreign influence
of the West and embrace their intrinsic connection to
the East and the primitive (Goncharova).
Khlebnikovs Stone Woman, written in 1919, is
a more somber piece that like Venus and the Shaman
functions as a commentary on the spiritual power of the
female figure.13 Here, however, the females sexuality is
secondary. Instead, it is her connection with nature and
eternity that gives the female figure power and allows
her to transcend human life and death.
Khlebnikov demonstrates the closeness of the
female figure to the natural world by selecting an
enchanted place, presumably far from civilization, as
the home of the Stone Woman. A Scythian stone idol,
she has stood lifeless and breathless in the same spot for
generations and is condemned to stand here forever
more. Her power is eternal and universal, stretching
from sky to sky.14 It is comparable only to the power
of the nature that surrounds her: The mountains whirl
in webs of snow, / unwindings of millennial sounds.
The mountains too are bound to stand here eternally
and have incomprehensible knowledge. Thus the Stone
Woman is surrounded by a grandiose natural landscape
and is one with it.
An anguished young man disturbs the stillness
and fairytale wonder by approaching the Stone Woman,
desperate for the idols comforting presence. He weeps
for all those who have died in wars and battles. Helpless
in the face of death, he feels like a miniscule speck in
the spectrum of time beating like a captured butterfly in
the meshes of the Milky Way. In contrast to this one
humans helpless position, the Stone Womans power is
boundless because of her connection to the earth and so
she transcends any single mortal life and death.
As the man weeps, a motha symbol of na-
turesuddenly lands on the idol bringing her to life.
Her transformation further emphasizes the connection
between the Stone Woman, nature, life, and death. The
transformative moment imbues the poem with the
vitality of life as the Stone Womans eyes flicker and
fill with intelligence while she breaks into a frenzied
dance. Khlebnikov describes her birth with imagery
of fire, but the life-giving moth is unlikely to survive
the flickering cherry stain. Furthermore, the Stone
Womans turbulent dance sharply contrasts with her
disciples mournful cries for the blood filling the Tisza
and Vistula rivers. Death and dance are juxtaposed be-
cause the female figures connection with nature, land,
and earth allow her to transcend the limits imposed on
humanity. Like Mother Nature or Mother Russia who is
eternal, universal, and all seeing, the Stone Woman is a
seer through the Milky Way. She will remain a source
of power, comfort, and inspiration for eternity regard-
less of how many individuals live or die.
This work can be read as a commentary on the
connection of Russian people. Even as mortal lives end,
their sprits are united by their shared history and idols,
FEATURE
which allows the cycle of life and death to continue. The
Stone Woman is a very different female figure than Ve-
nus. While Venus exudes life and sensuality, the Stone
Woman is coarse and lifeless. But they share a common
spirita sprit that transcends everyday life and cant
be tamed or even understood. And it is this strength of
spirit upon which the Futurists believed that national
strength and identity should be fashioned.
Like Khlebnikovs poem, Natalia Goncharovas
1908 painting Stone Woman also depicts the Scythian
stone sculpture. But in Goncharovas Stone Woman
she strives to bring the extraordinarythe idolinto
everyday life by situating the Stone Woman in the role
of a nude model. The Stone Woman, though she is
inanimate, has a very dynamic role in this piece as she
destabilizes several norms by actively redefining her
representation.
The Stone Woman is not the traditional Western
representation of beauty as she is far from the volup-
tuous, milk-skinned nude. Instead, Goncharova assigns
this role to an inanimate, crude, and distinctly primitive
stone sculpture, thereby replacing the Western ideal of
beauty with the other. Goncharova uses modern-
ist techniques of flattening and figural distortion to
emphasize how distant the Stone Woman is from the
Western ideal of beauty.
The Stone Woman has no neck and instead her
smooth oval head is pasted onto her torso. Her facial
features are somewhat blurred, with half-closed eyes
that appear as thin slits. A long nose runs down the
length of her face and meets thin, slightly pursed lips.
Willowy arms extend from comparatively broad and
muscular shoulders. The same stark contrast is repeated
by the tiny feet, which extend from disproportion-
ably full thighs. Unlike the typical female nude, this
female figure is desexualized although she is naked. Not
sprawled on a bed fully exposed, she is, instead, com-
pressed in a fetal-like position with legs tucked up to her
torso, arms held protectively over her flattened rather
than voluptuous chest.
In addition to defying what the nude model
should look like, the Stone Woman reimagines the role
of the model. Next to Stone Woman appear painters
brushes, behind her is a canvas with flowers, and in
her hands she holds a small tubepossibly a tube of
paint. The canvas and painterly tools suggest that she is
both model and artist. Thus the Stone Woman refuses
to conform to what is proper and expected; instead she
takes a very active role in redefining and reinventing.
Not only does she defy the traditional representation of
beauty, but she reinvents the role of the passive model
by actively participating in the act of creating. The
Stone Womans refusal to be confined to a certain kind
of representation accurately aligns with the goals of the
NORTHWESTERN UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH JOURNAL
FEATURE
Futurists, as this is the same active participation they
proposed for the construction of a Russian national
identity.
Unlike Stone Woman, which straddles the lines
between the extraordinary and the mundane, in Plant-
ing Potatoes, completed around 1909, Goncharova is
fully situated in the world of familiar subject matter.
The female figure is no longer the divine being of the
Stone Woman or the goddess Venus, but is an ordinary
peasant working in the fields. By capturing an indefinite
moment in the everyday life of the Russian peasant,
Goncharova romanticizes hard work and the ordinary,
demonstrating her interest in heroizing and mytholo-
gizing the mundane. While the works discussed above
primarily explored the female figures spiritual strength,
in this painting, the womens physical strength is most
significant.
Although Goncharova has not adopted total
abstraction, in the modernist style, she has rejected
traditional realism and distorts the human form to
emphasize certain elements of the piece. Without the
use of modeling and shading, Goncharova depicts the
women as flattened and geometric with disproportion-
ately large hands and feet. Their shovels, on the other
hand, appear diminutive in contrast to their towering
bodies. The scale and strength of the womens physical-
ity demonstrates that they dont lead lives of leisure but
have adapted to long hours of strenuous work. Suggest-
ing that these peasant women are intimately tied to the
land on which they work, their feet are like thick roots
firmly planted into their domestic soil. In the distance
appears the paintings only male figure. Smaller and fur-
ther away, his inclusion again underscores the womens
closeness to the land and implies that they are able to
wok independently of men.
With olive skin tone and dark eyes, the womens
sharp, angular facial feature dont appear to be Eu-
ropean or even Eastern European. Closer to the the
true face of peasant RussiaAsiatic and Scythian, the
women represent the Russian other that the Futurists
idolized (State 12). Red headscarves, traditionally worn
by female peasantry, explicitly stress their Russian-
ness. Notably, Goncharova is not depicting a portrait
of specific women at a particular moment in time. This
can be inferred because the womens faces lack detail
and individualization, their clothes cannot be dated,
and their location cannot be ascertained. In creating an
ambiguous time and space within the painting, Gon-
charova intends these laborers to represent all peasant
woman hard at work in the fields at all moments of
Russian history.
Planting Potatoes is particularly compelling
because the peasant women arent overly romanti-
cized. They are not lovely, sensuous maidens leisurely
NORTHWESTERN UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH JOURNAL
sprawled on a luscious pasture as their cattle graze
nearby. Neither clean nor pretty, their work demands
that they toil with shovels, lug heavy bags of potatoes,
and soil their coarse, bare feet. Goncharova is not just
idolizing the primitive, she is idolizing and heroiz-
ing the hard work of the primitive. Greatly valuing
labor, Goncharova reportedly said that Everything
passesfriendship and love; the only thing that remains
is work, (State 10). Strong, independent, and timeless,
these female peasants personify a nation built on hard,
Russian work.
The binaries of the divine and mundane, estab-
lished by Khelbnikov and Goncahrova, are reconciled
in Larionovs Jewish Venus from 1912. By depicting a
naked army prostitute confidently prostrated on a bed,
Jewish Venus instills the divine qualities of the untamed
sexuality and spirit of Venus into a mortal form. This
piece also demonstrates Larionovs interest in blur-
ring the distinctions of high and low art by portraying
classes, races, and ethnicities typically dismissed by the
Academy.
Like Goncharova, Larionov plays with realistic
representation by rendering the prostitute as flattened
with large and exaggerated facial features. She is fully
nude yet, like Khlebnikovs Venus, she is not ashamed of
her nudity nor is she portrayed in a position of victim-
ization. She is defiant, boldly staring at the viewer as she
shamelessly displays photographs of soldiersher cli-
entstriumphantly pasted on the wall behind her. Her
collection of client photographs is empowering because
it demonstrates that the prostitute is not ashamed of her
position in life. On the contrary, she collects mementos
to commemorate her conquests. The photographs can
also be read as a commentary on the Nemprimitivists
stance on technology and modernity. Although photog-
raphy was not a particularly new invention at this time,
it nonetheless represents technology and innovation. Its
inclusion in this work reaffirms that the Futurists were
not interested in rejecting modernization but wanted
progress to proceed on Russian terms.
According to Parton, the prostitutes defiant gaze
and the stark pallor of her skin against a bright green
wall are direct references to Edouard Manets Olympia
(52). But Larionovs Venus is no frail, high-class cour-
tesan. She has a peasants physicality with large, strong
arms and feet. A peasant prostitute, she could easily
spend her days as one of Goncharovas potato planters.
Depicting the female with what Larionov per-
ceived as distinctly Jewish features reveals his interest in
exploring the ethnological canons of beauty (Parton
52). Larionov studied ethnography and was particularly
interested in the themes of racial characteristics. He
wanted to uncover the unique features that different
ethnic groups use to measure the standards of beauty.
Armed with this alternative beauty vocabulary, Larionov
strives to challenge Western ideals of perfection (Parton
The rejection of European high art is further
asserted by the single red rose that appears on the wall
next to the soldiers photographs. Parton suggests that
the rose is a reference to the Greek myth of Venus and
Adonis (Parton 109). By referencing the classical Venus,
Larionov is emphasizing that he is reimagining the ide-
al. The divine goddess is brought to earth and becomes
the earthly and tangible goddess of love (Parton 52).
But not only is the divine or academic Venus made
obsolete and the West dusted off, but the notions of
love, passion, and sensuality are now embodied in a
Russian peasant prostitute (Goncharova).
Although the female figure appears in several
manifestations in the works I have discussed, she main-
tains certain core characteristics in every reincarnation.
From the Stone Woman to the Jewish Venus, the female
figure is strong, empowered, and authentic. She is repre-
sented as raw and unrefined, bears who she is proudly,
and is in control of how she is perceived. The construc-
tion of national identity based on core, unrefined values
is an empowering philosophy and opens up research
opportunities in a variety of fields.
Conclusion
The role of the powerful female cultural hero makes
Neoprimitivism a rich period of study for feminist
and gender critics because it proposes a new model of
feminist identity in which the woman is not just an im-
age of fertility, but an image of strength and power. The
Futurist philosophy is particularly interesting because
they were not making a comparison of the male and
female strength. Rather than propose that the female is
as strong as a men, the Futurists asserted that the female
is strong independently of men.
Unfortunately, the empowered role of the woman
can also have destabilizing consequences because of the
potential tensions between strength/liberated sexuality
and fertility/motherhood. In a world where the role of
the woman is to be more than a mother, what happens
to the sanctity of motherhood? Can the sexually liber-
ated, empowered Jewish Venus also be a strong mother
figure?
Beyond the role of the female figure, this project
has stakes for Art Historians. Russian Futurism was
one of the first times that Russia became a leader and
innovator in the visual arts (Gray 94). With the founda-
tion established by the groundbreaking and progressive
innovations of Larionov and Goncharoav, younger
Russian artists had a basis upon which to structure their
theories. Some of these theories, including Malevich
Suprematism, attained more recognition in the West,
FEATURE
but the Futurists were instrumental in introducing
Russia to the global art conversation. Additionally, this
was a unique period in Russian Art History because the
visual arts preceded and led literature, as most innova-
tions were first made visually and then replicated in
poetry. Typically in the history of Russian culture, this
relationship was reversed and literature paved the way
for visual developments (Gray 108).
Finally, the study of the Futurists quest for
national identity can add value to cultural studies. The
Futurists wanted Russia to reject dominant world-
views and fashion a national identity based on her own
culture and values. They were fully invested in figuring
out how to be progressive and forward thinking while
preserving Russian culture and history. Maintaining cul-
tural independence is a vital and challenging question
even todayperhaps more than ever todaybecause
of the homogenization of values and ideas fueled by
globalization and global communication. The Futurists
offer one empowering method of deriving indepen-
dence by introspectively identifying sources of national
strength such as the female was for Russia.

STRANDED
IN JORDAN:
A Study of Jordans Iraqi Refugee Policy
Laura Ashbaugh
INTERNATIONAL STUDIES PROGRAM
Galya Ruffer
FACULTY ADVISOR
INTERNATIONAL STUDIES PROGRAM
NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY
Jacqueline McAllister
Photo by Eva Serna
GRADUATE STUDENT MENTOR
DEPARTMENT OF POLITICAL SCIENCE
NORTHWESTERN UNIVERSITY
The refugee policies of first world countries and the international
refugee regime have been popular topics in refugee studies. This
research often overlooks that most refugees flee to neighboring
countries in the third world and minimizes the impact that these
countries’ domestic policies have on the refugees. The literature on
host countries’ responses to a refugee influx is based on a different
context than is most often found in the developing world. With one
of the highest ratios of refugees to total population in the world,
Jordan challenges the standard assumptions and theories in the literature. Jordan has an authoritarian regime, a chronic lack of natural
and economic resources, an insular and homogeneous society, a
complex diplomatic position in the region and vis-à-vis the U.S., and
a complicated history of hosting Palestinian refugees. This research
traces the historical trajectory of Jordanian policies on Iraqi refugees
and explains them as rational reactions to the refugees’ perceived
impact on Jordan’s external relations, regime security, and socioeconomic situation. Elements of process tracing, content analysis,
and discourse analysis are employed to examine official discourse
on Iraqi refugees in speeches, interviews, and press reports. Its findings suggest that despite continued discourse on treating Iraqis as
“welcomed guests,” the Jordanian regime’s tightening policies reveal increasing concern that the refugees’ presence is a threat to the
security and stability of the regime and Jordanian society. Furthermore, the policies reflect the regime’s chronic fear of weakness and
its desire to preserve social and political homogeneity.
FEATURE
T
he Middle East’s ‘Other’ Refugee Problem
Academics and policymakers alike have
been troubled by the dramatic increase in
the number of refugees and forced migrants
worldwide over the past several decades. De-
veloping countries with limited resources are absorbing
massive influxes of refugees without durable solutions
to their resettlement or repatriation. Jordan is a prime
example of this problem. Between 450,000 and 750,000
Iraqi refugees are estimated to be living in urban areas
in Jordan, adding considerably to its small population
of six million.1 While receiving minimal international
attention, the Iraqi displacement after the U.S. invasion
in 2003 is in fact larger than the size of the Palestinian
flight in 1948.2  Jordans capital city, Amman, now has
the distinction of having the most refugees of any city
in the world, according to a 2010 study released by the
United Nations.3 Jordanians reactions to the influx
of Iraqis have been mixed. Initially, the spirit of Arab
brotherhood and the strong historical ties between the
people of Iraq and Jordan compelled hospitality. Later,
Jordanians blamed Iraqis for inflation, housing short-
ages, high food prices, and job scarcity.4 This frustration
was expressed not just in public discourse, but also in
sporadic violence against Iraqis.5
Until now, much of the focus and research on
Iraqi refugees has been on temporary humanitar-
ian assistance and the possibilities of resettlement or
repatriation. Researchers, policymakers, and the United
Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR)
consider voluntary repatriation as the ideal solution
for refugees. Despite the tenuous security situation in
Iraq, there is pressure from around the world to repa-
triate Iraqi refugees. European countries have begun
deporting Iraqi refugees who did not qualify for asylum,
and Middle Eastern countries are eager to ease the strain
on their resources.6 King Abdullah II of Jordan has
repeatedly said that his country does not want another
permanent refugee population because of the burden
on its resources, water, education, and health systems.7
Despite the increasing clamor for Iraqis to return to
their country, few have moved back. In the first six
months of 2009, only 150 out of 500,000 Iraqis living in
Jordan repatriated with UNHCR assistance, according
to a study published in July 2009.8 According to the UN
study, Iraqis reportedly felt that current conditions in
Iraq prevented them from returning home, and many
said they would not return under any circumstance. The
study quoted a Jordanian scholar saying, The decision
to flee from your own country is always easier to make
than the decision to return.  With no end in sight to
Jordans role as host to Iraqi refugees, it is crucial to
NORTHWESTERN UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH JOURNAL
understand Jordans refugee policies and their impacts
domestically, regionally, and internationally.
There is a plethora of research on international
organizations involvement in refugee situations, first
world countries responses to refugee crises, and on
resettlement processes of refugees in those first world
countries. There is much less research focusing on
the countries where most refugees flee to: developing
countries in the third world. Furthermore, there is little
attention on what shapes these countries responses
to refugees, and models based on developed Western
countries fail to explain the behavior of developing
nations such as Jordan.  For example, Myron Weiner,
an internationally recognized migration and security
scholar, has theorized that a countrys national secu-
rity and political interests trump its moral willingness
to accommodate refugees.9 Weiner posits that when a
country perceives a refugee influx as a threat to its se-
curity and stability, it will likely respond with economic
aid, coercive diplomacy, or armed intervention. Since
his analysis focuses on wealthy, industrial countries,
however, it does not adequately account for Jordans
behavior. Jordans unique historical and geopoliti-
cal position prevent it from responding to perceived
security threats according to Myrons or other scholars
models. Jordan has neither the economic might nor
diplomatic capital to prevent a refugee flow, and its
relationship with the U.S. makes a military intervention
in Iraq unthinkable. Jordans authoritarian government,
precarious location in a volatile region, and delicate
diplomatic position make it a unique case that defies the
mold created by Weiner and other scholars.  Thus, Jor-
dan responds in the few ways that it still can: tightening
border controls, discouraging assimilation, preventing
political participation, soliciting international aid, and
insisting on third country resettlement or repatriation.
Since developing countries like Jordan perceive a refu-
gee influx differently from those in the developed world,
explaining their behavior in response to a massive influx
of refugees requires a different model.  While their poli-
cies are often criticized as unnecessarily restrictive and
detrimental to refugees, the policies can be explained as
rational reactions to a perceived threat.
This research aims to offer a new model to explain
how we understand Jordans evolving refugee poli-
cies and conflicting discourses as a reflection of state
interests and rational choices.   Through analysis of
Jordanian policy documents, speeches, and interactions
with other nations and international organizations, this
research traces the evolution of Jordans perceptions
of the Iraqi refugees and explains its policy decisions
as actions to preserve the regimes security. For this
analysis, elements of process tracing, content analysis,
and discourse analysis were used. While fully employing
these techniques is beyond the scope of this project, the
methods have informed the qualitative analysis.  This
first research aim provides an analysis of the politi-
cal and historical context of Jordanian refugee policy,
with particular attention to its experience with Pales-
tinian refugees and its complicated relationship with
Iraq. Next, this research provides a detailed analysis
of Jordans evolving policy responses to Iraqi refugees,
dividing them by category and by their adherence to
internationally sanctioned recommendations. Finally, it
offers an explanation of how these policies were made
in response to perceived security and stability threats.
Jordans refugee policy choices are reactions to a dete-
riorating economic situation, growing domestic unrest,
continuing terrorist threats, and dwindling resources.
Center of the Storm: How Jordan Became the
Region’s Safe Haven
In order to understand Jordans current predicament
with Iraqi refugees, it is necessary to appreciate its his-
tory. In just 90 years since its state formation, Jordan has
transformed from a sparsely populated desert to an im-
portant regional player.  Jordan has been widely called
an artificial state that has historically been plagued by
dire resource scarcity and weak political power.  With
a leader brought in from the Hijaz and a hodgepodge
population of Bedouin, its political survival following
its creation in the wake of World War I seemed unlikely
at best. Jordan has persevered because of the tenacity of
its political elites, the loyalty of the East Bank security
establishment, and the countrys geopolitical centrality.
These are still the three factors that keep the Hashemite
regime in power in Jordan today.10
In addition, Jordan has had a tumultuous history
with its neighbor, Iraq. Iraqi refugees are only one factor
in the power plays between Jordan and the new govern-
ment in Iraq. Throughout most of its history, Jordan
has had close economic and social ties with Iraq, and
the Jordanian people have often sided with Iraq even
before their own monarch. The break in relations in
the decade preceding the U.S. invasion of Iraq and the
subsequent change of regime dramatically changed the
dynamic. Nevertheless, Jordan was the first Arab coun-
try to send an ambassador to Baghdad following the in-
vasion and has constantly rallied support for Iraqs new
government in the Arab League.11 The burden of host-
ing so many Iraqis, however, has increasingly become
part of the official discourse between Iraq and Jordan.
Eager to repatriate the Iraqis, Jordan has a significant
interest in catalyzing the stability and security of Iraq.
Jordan has a long history of addressing refugee is-
sues. Since 1948, Jordan has hosted millions of Palestin-
ian refugees, who now make up about 60 percent of the
countrys population. In 1950, King Hussein annexed
FEATURE
the West Bank and gave Palestinians Jordanian citizen-
ship, making Jordan the only Arab country to confer
widespread citizenship rights to Palestinians.12  Like
most other Arab countries, Jordan is not a signatory to
the United Nations 1951 Convention on the Status of
Refugees and its 1967 Protocol, meaning that it does not
legally recognize refugees nor offer them the full protec-
tion and rights under the convention. Historically, Arab
countries did not sign the convention because they
argued that the convention did not adequately preserve
the Palestinians right of return and self-determina-
tion.13 Consequently, many Arab countries have large
refugee populations, but lack the formal protections and
legal systems to process those refugees. An additional
consequence is that Arab governments have an aversion
to using the term refugee for non-Palestinian refugees
in Middle East: the government of Jordan, for example,
officially calls Iraqis guests or visitors, and in the
Arab press the Iraqis are often called the displaced or
immigrants.14
Humanitarian organizations have sought to draw
attention to the current Iraqi refugee crisis by calling
it unprecedented, but this obscures the fact that Iraq
has a long history of forced migration that is deeply in-
grained in the regions political history. This most recent
flight of Iraqis into other Middle Eastern countries can
be considered to be simply an amplification and con-
tinuation of preexisting regional migration patterns.  All
of Iraqs neighbors - and especially Iran, Turkey, Jordan,
and Syria - have received waves of forced migrants over
the decades because of successive Iraqi regimes at-
tempts to exert control over the population by restrict-
ing their mobility and fragmenting them along political,
ethnic, religious, or ideological lines.15 Since 1991, Iraq
hemorrhaged between 4.2 and 4.8 million internal and
external refugees, accounting for more than a fifth of its
total population.  Millions of Iraqis came into Jordan
throughout the 1990s, but due to the expense and
difficulty of the journey, those who arrived in Jordan
were mainly a self-selected group who were well-edu-
cated and upper-middle class.16 Jordan traditionally
received those fleeing instability in Iraq as temporary
guests, not refugees, based on the regional tradition
of Pan-Arabism.17 Jordan also served an important role
as a transit country, as many Iraqis left Jordan to seek
asylum in Europe or the U.S. Thus, while many Iraqis in
Jordan are indeed stranded and living in Jordan illegally,
the population is by no means universally static. These
migration patterns are important because they con-
tribute to the Jordanian governments refusal to either
recognize Iraqis as a refugee population or to treat
them according to international standards.
Reliable information on the number of Iraqis who
returned to Iraq without UNHCR assistance is hard

The Evolution of Jordan’s Iraqi Refugee Policy
In order to trace Jordans evolving refugee policies,
this research adopts Jacobsens method of categorizing
Jordans policies as either positive (UN recommended)
or negative, and by their type: legal-bureaucratic,
limiting international organizations activities, and the
admission or treatment of refugees. These policies were
further evaluated as containing positive or negative
elements, with positive responses being in perfect accor-
dance with internationally sanctioned refugee policies.
Next, the cause of these policies is explained by adopt-
ing Weiners framework for analyzing how host coun-
tries perceive refugee populations as a security/stability
threat. His factors can be condensed into three areas of
analysis for this case study: how the Iraqi refugees affect
Jordans external relations, the security of the Jordanian
regime itself, and the social and economic conditions in
Jordan (referred to as absorptive capacity by Gorden-
ker22, Stein23, and Jacobsen24). Analyzing Jordan under
this combined framework shows that Jordan perceives
the Iraqi refugees as a security and stability threat and
responds in ways that are not predicted by models based
on Western or developed countries. Jordans unique his-
torical context and geopolitical position mean that the
responses available to Jordan are discouraging assimila-
tion, preventing political participation, soliciting inter-
national aid, and insisting on third country resettlement
or repatriation.
Jordans policy toward Iraqi refugees has evolved
as the crisis has evolved. As part of a well-established
NORTHWESTERN UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH JOURNAL
regional migration pattern, Iraqi emigration is neither a
new nor shocking phenomenon, which is perhaps why
Jordan and its neighbors did not respond at first to the
2003 influx with a dramatic change in policy. Instead,
the policy only shifted when the Iraqi population began
to be perceived as a security and stability threat to the
Jordanian regime.  Jordans legal and bureaucratic
policies can be categorized as negative because Jordan
has not adopted international refugee law and has no
legal framework for determining the status of refu-
gees. Although Jordan has a plethora of institutions
and agencies to support Palestinian refugees, it lacks
a comparable bureaucratic structure to address Iraqi
refugee issues. However, this is more indicative of the
adverse political implications of acknowledging an Iraqi
refugee population than of Jordans lack of experience
with refugee matters. Furthermore, Jordan considers
Iraqis to be guests, not refugees or asylum seek-
ers because of its complicated history with Palestinian
refugees.  As for its relationship with IROs, Jordan has
generally had positive responses by welcoming their aid
and allowing full access, but it has also restricted some
of their programming to ensure that it also benefits
poor Jordanians.
In the third policy category of admission and
treatment, Jordan has had progressively more negative
responses.  There was no radical shift in refugee policy
in the immediate aftermath of the invasion of Iraq, but
the practical problems of hosting hundreds of thou-
sands of refugees soon required policy responses. Jorda-
nian policies were described generally as quite generous
in the period between 2003 and 2005.  Most Iraqis at the
border were given visas and allowed to enter. After 2005,
social services were extended to Iraqis, particularly
public education and reduced costs for medical services.
Work permits are hard to come by and about 80 percent
of Iraqis lack proper residence permits. As they fell into
illegality, Iraqis were reluctant to seek out those social
services for fear of deportation. Increasing entry restric-
tions, often based on discriminatory factors like age or
religion, are other examples of negative responses.  Still,
there have been no large-scale deportations or com-
plaints of involuntary repatriation.
Jordanian Perceptions of Iraqi Refugees as a
Security/Stability Threat
The evolving refugee policies can be explained as a
rational response to the security and stability threat
perceived by the Jordanian government. Exploring the
internal dynamics of Jordan  the insecurity of the
regime, domestic unrest, economic problems, and social
tensions  offers an explanation for why the Jordanian
regime views Iraqi refugees as a security/stability threat
and why it would depart from its period of open door
migration and its policy of no policy.  The refugees
have impacted Jordanian international relations, the
security of the regime, and the socioeconomic climate.
The presence of Iraqi refugees has meant that Jordan
has a vital interest in restoring Iraqs strength and
stability, and has provided a strong impetus for forming
close ties with the new Iraqi government. Regionally,
the presence of Iraqi refugees has reinforced Jordans
self-constructed role as a safe haven for regional refu-
gees and a champion of Arab brotherhood. The Iraqi
refugees are an unspoken problem between Jordan and
the U.S. because their presence is evidence of the poor
security situation in Iraq. The refugees have proved to
be useful leverage for Jordan in making the case for in-
creased international aid, which in turn can be diverted
for domestic priorities.
As for the threat to the unity of Jordanian society,
the Iraqi refugees are perceived as visible evidence of
the spread of the Shiite Crescent and as a constant
reminder of the fact that allowing foreigners into the
country can expose innocent civilians to terrorist at-
tacks. Furthermore, Weiners theory of security as a
social construct proved true for this case study: in a ho-
mogeneous society like Jordan where the regime gains
its legitimacy from its religious and ethnic leadership,
an influx of newcomers destabilizes Jordanian unity,
and thus the regimes grip on power.  Since Iraqi refu-
gees are seen as a source of terrorism and political desta-
bilization, the Jordanian government has responded by
repressing domestic opposition and political participa-
tion, which only contributes to the cycle of instability
and insecurity.
Furthermore, the influx of Iraqis proved to be a
convenient, but unfounded scapegoat for socioeconom-
ic woes, allowing the Jordanian regime to deflect blame
for the economic hardship caused by the Iraq War
(in which the regime was a complicit partner) to the
relatively blameless flood of Iraqi refugees.25  Domestic
opposition grows as the Jordanian regime fails to solve
the high unemployment rates and the rising prices of
gas and food. Furthermore, with Iraqis perceived among
the general public as the source of all those problems,
their continued presence, and the possibility of their
permanent residence, provides a flashpoint for domestic
unrest. Thus the Jordanian regime uses the foreign aid
intended to assist the Iraqi refugees to consolidate gov-
ernmental institutions and its own power. Regardless
of the degree of their actual impact, the perception of
the Jordanian government and its people is that Iraqis
threaten their security and stability. Therefore, Jordans
departure from its historical approach to migration
and refugees is not an unexplainable aberration, but a
rational response to perceived threats.
FEATURE
The Future of Iraqi Refugees in Jordan
Since the likelihood of an extended, if not permanent,
stay in Jordan for Iraqi refugees grows higher with news
of every bombing and election snafu in Iraq, Jordans
policy choices continue to have a significant impact on
the lives and futures of Iraqi refugees. The refugee prob-
lem grows more urgent every day; hundreds of thou-
sands of Iraqi refugees are still stranded in Jordan, with
their personal resources dwindling and with limited
access to work, education and healthcare. The majority
of Iraqis are living illegally and fear both deportation
and the uncertain future.
Voluntary repatriation is considered by the UN to
be the ideal solution for any refugee population, but it is
rarely practical or achievable, and has in fact never been
enacted en masse.26  The continuing violence in Iraq,
its political instability, and the vast internally displaced
population are all challenges to repatriation. Most Iraqis
have no desire to return to their country anytime soon
because of the continuing violence in Iraq and because
many dont have homes to return to: sectarian violence
in religiously mixed areas of Iraq led to vast internal
displacement and the formation of new, ethnically
homogeneous communities. The controversies and alle-
gations of fraud surrounding the March 2010 elections
have also undermined political stability, and violence
still plagues the country.  Local resettlement, considered
to be the next best alternative, is problematic in host
countries like Jordan with low absorptive capacity, deep
political and security concerns, and vocal opposition to
such a prospect. Jordan has made it abundantly clear
that it is not willing to be host to another permanent
refugee population. The potential for a permanent
Iraqi refugee population threatens Jordans security and
stability, and therefore the Jordanian government has
made no plans for long-term resettlement or assimila-
tion in Jordan.  Third-country resettlement, the next
best alternative, is also not realistic given the aversion in
Europe and the U.S. to accepting a refugee population
with whom it has little ethnic affinity. These countries
prefer funneling aid to regional host countries over
opening their own borders to refugees. Thus, the Iraqi
refugees pose a dilemma to which there is no clear solu-
tion, and their humanitarian needs are only worsening
with the passage of time. An understanding of how
Jordans refugee policies are made, however, is crucial to
evaluating the future of Iraqi refugees in Jordan.

OBJECT IDENTIFICATION
FUNCTIONAL ATTRIBUTES
People have a fascinating ability to identify individual objects and keep
track of them even through dramatic changes over time. In this study, we
investigated the identity preservation of individual objects with a specific
focus on functional attributes. Participants were asked to imagine a flawed
copy machine, which took an object and produced an altered version of it,
along with other modified copies. A picture of the original object, which
was given a name and a functional attribute, was presented to the participants followed by several of the outputs, and participants were asked
to judge whether outputs could be identified as the original object. We
found that if the original object and the output shared the same functional
attribute, people were significantly more likely to say that it could be the
original object and that identity was preserved. We also found that identity was preserved less with increasing transformational distance between
the object and the output, a seemingly intuitive trend but one that has not
been consistently produced in literature.

Introduction
Suppose that you have lost your keys sometime during the day. Later your coworker says she
found them, and drops a set of keys into your hand. How do you know if they are your keys?
Would it be convincing enough for them to physically resemble your keys? What if they looked
different, but could still be used to open your front door? Everyday, people resolve these kinds
of problems that require tracking the identity of individual objects. But how do we solve these
problems and what kinds of information do we rely on to solve them?
Current theories offer competing accounts for how people determine the identity of
an individual object. Perhaps the most intuitive possibility is that people rely on perceptual
similarity to match a recovered object to the original object. However, previous research has
found that from a young age people usually choose a unique individual object that they have
formed a personal attachment to over an exact duplicate of it (Hood & Bloom, 2008). This
suggests that even young children use more than mere perceptual similarity in identifying
individual objects. Moreover, people can often easily tell that two very similar looking objects
are different, and that two very different looking objects are the same. For example, identical
twin sisters can be identified as two different individuals even though they look extremely
similar, and we can also tell that even though we met cousin Laura as a baby, she is still the
same cousin now even though she is a teenager.
